9: ---
10: 
11: In Next.js, routes are rendered on the server by default. This often means the client has to wait for a server response before a new route can be shown. Next.js comes with built-in [prefetching](#prefetching), [streaming](#streaming), and [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions) ensuring navigation stays fast and responsive.
12: 
13: This guide explains how navigation works in Next.js and how you can optimize it for [dynamic routes](#dynamic-routes-without-loadingtsx) and [slow networks](#slow-networks).
14: 
15: ## How navigation works
16: 
17: To understand how navigation works in Next.js, it helps to be familiar with the following concepts:
18: 
19: - [Server Rendering](#server-rendering)
20: - [Prefetching](#prefetching)
21: - [Streaming](#streaming)
22: - [Client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions)
23: 
24: ### Server Rendering
25: 
26: In Next.js, [Layouts and Pages](/docs/app/getting-started/layouts-and-pages) are [React Server Components](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components) by default. On initial and subsequent navigations, the [Server Component Payload](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#how-do-server-and-client-components-work-in-nextjs) is generated on the server before being sent to the client.
27: 
28: There are two types of server rendering, based on _when_ it happens:
29: 
30: - **Prerendering** happens at build time or during [revalidation](/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating) and the result is cached.
31: - **Dynamic Rendering** happens at request time in response to a client request.
32: 
33: The trade-off of server rendering is that the client must wait for the server to respond before the new route can be shown. Next.js addresses this delay by [prefetching](#prefetching) routes the user is likely to visit and performing [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions).
34: 
35: > **Good to know**: HTML is also generated for the initial visit.
36: 
37: ### Prefetching
38: 
39: Prefetching is the process of loading a route in the background before the user navigates to it. This makes navigation between routes in your application feel instant, because by the time a user clicks on a link, the data to render the next route is already available client side.
40: 
41: Next.js automatically prefetches routes linked with the [`<Link>` component](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link) when they enter the user's viewport.
42: 
43: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
44: import Link from 'next/link'
45: 
46: export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
47:   return (
48:     <html>
49:       <body>
50:         <nav>
51:           {/* Prefetched when the link is hovered or enters the viewport */}
52:           <Link href="/blog">Blog</Link>
53:           {/* No prefetching */}
54:           <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
55:         </nav>
56:         {children}
57:       </body>
58:     </html>
59:   )
60: }
61: ```
62: 
63: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
64: import Link from 'next/link'
65: 
66: export default function Layout({ children }) {
67:   return (
68:     <html>
69:       <body>
70:         <nav>
71:           {/* Prefetched when the link is hovered or enters the viewport */}
72:           <Link href="/blog">Blog</Link>
73:           {/* No prefetching */}
74:           <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
75:         </nav>
76:         {children}
77:       </body>
78:     </html>
79:   )
80: }
81: ```
82: 
83: How much of the route is prefetched depends on whether it's static or dynamic:
84: 
85: - **Static Route**: the full route is prefetched.
86: - **Dynamic Route**: prefetching is skipped, or the route is partially prefetched if [`loading.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) is present.
87: 
88: By skipping or partially prefetching dynamic routes, Next.js avoids unnecessary work on the server for routes the users may never visit. However, waiting for a server response before navigation can give the users the impression that the app is not responding.
89: 
90: <Image
91:   alt="Server Rendering without Streaming"
92:   srcLight="/docs/light/server-rendering-without-streaming.png"
93:   srcDark="/docs/dark/server-rendering-without-streaming.png"
94:   width="1600"
95:   height="748"
96: />
97: 
98: > **Good to know:** See the [Prefetching guide](/docs/app/guides/prefetching) for the full behavior, including how to control prefetching per link and how it changes when you adopt [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching).
99: 
100: To improve the navigation experience to dynamic routes, you can use [streaming](#streaming).
101: 
102: ### Streaming
103: 
104: Streaming allows the server to send parts of a dynamic route to the client as soon as they're ready, rather than waiting for the entire route to be rendered. This means users see something sooner, even if parts of the page are still loading. See the [Streaming guide](/docs/app/guides/streaming) for a deep dive into how streaming works in Next.js.
105: 
106: For dynamic routes, it means they can be **partially prefetched**. That is, shared layouts and loading skeletons can be requested ahead of time.
107: 
108: <Image
109:   alt="How Server Rendering with Streaming Works"
110:   srcLight="/docs/light/server-rendering-with-streaming.png"
111:   srcDark="/docs/dark/server-rendering-with-streaming.png"
112:   width="1600"
113:   height="785"
114: />
115: 
116: To use streaming, create a `loading.tsx` in your route folder:
117: 
118: <Image
119:   alt="loading.js special file"
120:   srcLight="/docs/light/loading-special-file.png"
121:   srcDark="/docs/dark/loading-special-file.png"
122:   width="1600"
123:   height="606"
124: />
125: 
126: ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/loading.tsx" switcher
127: export default function Loading() {
128:   // Add fallback UI that will be shown while the route is loading.
129:   return <LoadingSkeleton />
130: }
131: ```
132: 
133: ```jsx filename="app/dashboard/loading.js" switcher
134: export default function Loading() {
135:   // Add fallback UI that will be shown while the route is loading.
136:   return <LoadingSkeleton />
137: }
138: ```
139: 
140: Behind the scenes, Next.js will automatically wrap the `page.tsx` contents in a `<Suspense>` boundary. The prefetched fallback UI will be shown while the route is loading, and swapped for the actual content once ready.
141: 
142: > **Good to know**: You can also use [`<Suspense>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) to create loading UI for nested components.
143: 
144: Benefits of `loading.tsx`:
145: 
146: - Immediate navigation and visual feedback for the user.
147: - Shared layouts remain interactive and navigation is interruptible.
148: - Improved Core Web Vitals: [TTFB](https://web.dev/articles/ttfb), [FCP](https://web.dev/articles/fcp), and [TTI](https://web.dev/articles/tti).
149: 
150: To further improve the navigation experience, Next.js performs a [client-side transition](#client-side-transitions) with the `<Link>` component.
151: 
152: ### Client-side transitions
153: 
154: Traditionally, navigation to a server-rendered page triggers a full page load. This clears state, resets scroll position, and blocks interactivity.
155: 
156: Next.js avoids this with client-side transitions using the `<Link>` component. Instead of reloading the page, it updates the content dynamically by:
157: 
158: - Keeping any shared layouts and UI.
159: - Replacing the current page with the prefetched loading state or a new page if available.
160: 
161: Client-side transitions are what makes a server-rendered apps _feel_ like client-rendered apps. And when paired with [prefetching](#prefetching) and [streaming](#streaming), it enables fast transitions, even for dynamic routes.
162: 
163: Next.js also handles [scrolling to the top of the page](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#scroll) during client-side transitions. If content scrolls behind a sticky or fixed header after navigation, you can fix this with CSS [`scroll-padding-top`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#scroll-offset-with-sticky-headers).
164: 
165: ## What can make transitions slow?
166: 
167: These Next.js optimizations make navigation fast and responsive. However, under certain conditions, transitions can still _feel_ slow. Here are some common causes and how to improve the user experience:
168: 
169: ### Dynamic routes without `loading.tsx`
170: 
171: When navigating to a dynamic route, the client must wait for the server response before showing the result. This can give the users the impression that the app is not responding.
172: 
173: We recommend adding `loading.tsx` to dynamic routes to enable partial prefetching, trigger immediate navigation, and display a loading UI while the route renders.
174: 
175: ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/loading.tsx" switcher
176: export default function Loading() {
177:   return <LoadingSkeleton />
178: }
179: ```
180: 
181: ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/loading.js" switcher
182: export default function Loading() {
183:   return <LoadingSkeleton />
184: }
185: ```
186: 
187: > **Good to know**: In development mode, you can use the Next.js Devtools to identify if the route is static or dynamic. See [`devIndicators`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/devIndicators) for more information.
188: 
189: ### Dynamic segments without `generateStaticParams`
190: 
191: If a [dynamic segment](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes) could be prerendered but isn't because it's missing [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params), the route will fallback to dynamic rendering at request time.
192: 
193: Ensure the route is statically generated at build time by adding `generateStaticParams`:
194: 
195: ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher
196: export async function generateStaticParams() {
197:   const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json())
198: 
199:   return posts.map((post) => ({
200:     slug: post.slug,
201:   }))
202: }
203: 
204: export default async function Page({
205:   params,
206: }: {
207:   params: Promise<{ slug: string }>
208: }) {
209:   const { slug } = await params
210:   // ...
211: }
212: ```
213: 
214: ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher
215: export async function generateStaticParams() {
216:   const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json())
217: 
218:   return posts.map((post) => ({
219:     slug: post.slug,
220:   }))
221: }
222: 
223: export default async function Page({ params }) {
224:   const { slug } = await params
225:   // ...
226: }
227: ```
228: 
229: ### Slow networks
230: 
231: On slow or unstable networks, prefetching may not finish before the user clicks a link. This can affect both static and dynamic routes. In these cases, the `loading.js` fallback may not appear immediately because it hasn't been prefetched yet.
232: 
233: To improve perceived performance, you can use the [`useLinkStatus` hook](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status) to show immediate feedback while the transition is in progress.
234: 
235: ```tsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.tsx" switcher
236: 'use client'
237: 
238: import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link'
239: 
240: export default function LoadingIndicator() {
241:   const { pending } = useLinkStatus()
242:   return (
243:     <span aria-hidden className={`link-hint ${pending ? 'is-pending' : ''}`} />
244:   )
245: }
246: ```
247: 
248: ```jsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.js" switcher
249: 'use client'
250: 
251: import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link'
252: 
253: export default function LoadingIndicator() {
254:   const { pending } = useLinkStatus()
255:   return (
256:     <span aria-hidden className={`link-hint ${pending ? 'is-pending' : ''}`} />
257:   )
258: }
259: ```
260: 
261: You can "debounce" the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. `opacity: 0`). This means the loading indicator will only be shown if the navigation takes longer than the specified delay. See the [`useLinkStatus` reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status#gracefully-handling-fast-navigation) for a CSS example.
262: 
263: > **Good to know**: An **experimental** [`useOffline`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/useOffline) hook can keep prefetched routes navigable during connectivity drops. See the [offline support guide](/docs/app/guides/offline-support).
264: 
265: > **Good to know**: You can use other visual feedback patterns like a progress bar. View an example [here](https://github.com/vercel/react-transition-progress).
266: 
267: ### Disabling prefetching
268: 
269: You can opt out of prefetching by setting the `prefetch` prop to `false` on the `<Link>` component. This is useful to avoid unnecessary usage of resources when rendering large lists of links (e.g. an infinite scroll table).
270: 
271: ```tsx
272: <Link prefetch={false} href="/blog">
273:   Blog
274: </Link>
275: ```
276: 
277: However, disabling prefetching comes with trade-offs:
278: 
279: - **Static routes** will only be fetched when the user clicks the link.
280: - **Dynamic routes** will need to be rendered on the server first before the client can navigate to it.
281: 
282: To reduce resource usage without fully disabling prefetch, you can prefetch only on hover. This limits prefetching to routes the user is more _likely_ to visit, rather than all links in the viewport.
283: 
284: ```tsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.tsx" switcher
285: 'use client'
286: 
287: import Link from 'next/link'
288: import { useState } from 'react'
289: 
290: function HoverPrefetchLink({
291:   href,
292:   children,
293: }: {
294:   href: string
295:   children: React.ReactNode
296: }) {
297:   const [active, setActive] = useState(false)
298: 
299:   return (
300:     <Link
301:       href={href}
302:       prefetch={active ? null : false}
303:       onMouseEnter={() => setActive(true)}
304:     >
305:       {children}
306:     </Link>
307:   )
308: }
309: ```
310: 
311: ```jsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.js" switcher
312: 'use client'
313: 
314: import Link from 'next/link'
315: import { useState } from 'react'
316: 
317: function HoverPrefetchLink({ href, children }) {
318:   const [active, setActive] = useState(false)
319: 
320:   return (
321:     <Link
322:       href={href}
323:       prefetch={active ? null : false}
324:       onMouseEnter={() => setActive(true)}
325:     >
326:       {children}
327:     </Link>
328:   )
329: }
330: ```
331: 
332: ### Hydration not completed
333: 
334: `<Link>` is a Client Component and must be hydrated before it can prefetch routes. On the initial visit, large JavaScript bundles can delay hydration, preventing prefetching from starting right away.
335: 
336: React mitigates this with Selective Hydration and you can further improve this by:
337: 
338: - Using the [`@next/bundle-analyzer`](/docs/app/guides/package-bundling#nextbundle-analyzer-for-webpack) plugin to identify and reduce bundle size by removing large dependencies.
339: - Moving logic from the client to the server where possible. See the [Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components) docs for guidance.
340: 
341: ## Examples
342: 
343: ### Native History API
344: 
345: Next.js allows you to use the native [`window.history.pushState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/pushState) and [`window.history.replaceState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState) methods to update the browser's history stack without reloading the page.
346: 
347: `pushState` and `replaceState` calls integrate into the Next.js Router, allowing you to sync with [`usePathname`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-pathname) and [`useSearchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-search-params).
348: 
349: #### `window.history.pushState`
350: 
351: Use it to add a new entry to the browser's history stack. The user can navigate back to the previous state. For example, to sort a list of products:
352: 
353: ```tsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.tsx" switcher
354: 'use client'
355: 
356: import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation'
357: 
358: export default function SortProducts() {
359:   const searchParams = useSearchParams()
360: 
361:   function updateSorting(sortOrder: string) {
362:     const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString())
363:     params.set('sort', sortOrder)
364:     window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`)
365:   }
366: 
367:   return (
368:     <>
369:       <button onClick={() => updateSorting('asc')}>Sort Ascending</button>
370:       <button onClick={() => updateSorting('desc')}>Sort Descending</button>
371:     </>
372:   )
373: }
374: ```
375: 
376: ```jsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.js" switcher
377: 'use client'
378: 
379: import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation'
380: 
381: export default function SortProducts() {
382:   const searchParams = useSearchParams()
383: 
384:   function updateSorting(sortOrder) {
385:     const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString())
386:     params.set('sort', sortOrder)
387:     window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`)
388:   }
389: 
390:   return (
391:     <>
392:       <button onClick={() => updateSorting('asc')}>Sort Ascending</button>
393:       <button onClick={() => updateSorting('desc')}>Sort Descending</button>
394:     </>
395:   )
396: }
397: ```
398: 
399: #### `window.history.replaceState`
400: 
401: Use it to replace the current entry on the browser's history stack. The user is not able to navigate back to the previous state. For example, to switch the application's locale:
402: 
403: ```tsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.tsx" switcher
404: 'use client'
405: 
406: import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation'
407: 
408: export function LocaleSwitcher() {
409:   const pathname = usePathname()
410: 
411:   function switchLocale(locale: string) {
412:     // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact'
413:     const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}`
414:     window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath)
415:   }
416: 
417:   return (
418:     <>
419:       <button onClick={() => switchLocale('en')}>English</button>
420:       <button onClick={() => switchLocale('fr')}>French</button>
421:     </>
422:   )
423: }
424: ```
425: 
426: ```jsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.js" switcher
427: 'use client'
428: 
429: import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation'
430: 
431: export function LocaleSwitcher() {
432:   const pathname = usePathname()
433: 
434:   function switchLocale(locale) {
435:     // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact'
436:     const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}`
437:     window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath)
438:   }
439: 
440:   return (
441:     <>
442:       <button onClick={() => switchLocale('en')}>English</button>
443:       <button onClick={() => switchLocale('fr')}>French</button>
444:     </>
445:   )
446: }
447: ```

2: title: Server and Client Components
3: description: Learn how you can use React Server and Client Components to render parts of your application on the server or the client.

10: 
11: By default, layouts and pages are [Server Components](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components), which lets you fetch data and render parts of your UI on the server, optionally cache the result, and stream it to the client. When you need interactivity or browser APIs, you can use [Client Components](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client) to layer in functionality.
12: 
13: This page explains how Server and Client Components work in Next.js and when to use them, with examples of how to compose them together in your application.
14: 
15: ## When to use Server and Client Components?
16: 
17: The client and server environments have different capabilities. Server and Client Components allow you to run logic in each environment depending on your use case.
18: 
19: Use **Client Components** when you need:
20: 
21: - [State](https://react.dev/learn/managing-state) and [event handlers](https://react.dev/learn/responding-to-events). E.g. `onClick`, `onChange`.
22: - [Lifecycle logic](https://react.dev/learn/lifecycle-of-reactive-effects). E.g. `useEffect`.
23: - Browser-only APIs. E.g. `localStorage`, `window`, `Navigator.geolocation`, etc.
24: - [Custom hooks](https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks).
25: 
26: Use **Server Components** when you need:
27: 
28: - Fetch data from databases or APIs close to the source.
29: - Use API keys, tokens, and other secrets without exposing them to the client.
30: - Reduce the amount of JavaScript sent to the browser.
31: - Improve the [First Contentful Paint (FCP)](https://web.dev/fcp/), and stream content progressively to the client.
32: 
33: For example, the `<Page>` component is a Server Component that fetches data about a post, and passes it as props to the `<LikeButton>` which handles client-side interactivity.
34: 
35: ```tsx filename="app/[id]/page.tsx" highlight={1,17} switcher
36: import LikeButton from '@/app/ui/like-button'
37: import { getPost } from '@/lib/data'
38: 
39: export default async function Page({
40:   params,
41: }: {
42:   params: Promise<{ id: string }>
43: }) {
44:   const { id } = await params
45:   const post = await getPost(id)
46: 
47:   return (
48:     <div>
49:       <main>
50:         <h1>{post.title}</h1>
51:         {/* ... */}
52:         <LikeButton likes={post.likes} />
53:       </main>
54:     </div>
55:   )
56: }
57: ```
58: 
59: ```jsx filename="app/[id]/page.js" highlight={1,12} switcher
60: import LikeButton from '@/app/ui/like-button'
61: import { getPost } from '@/lib/data'
62: 
63: export default async function Page({ params }) {
64:   const post = await getPost(params.id)
65: 
66:   return (
67:     <div>
68:       <main>
69:         <h1>{post.title}</h1>
70:         {/* ... */}
71:         <LikeButton likes={post.likes} />
72:       </main>
73:     </div>
74:   )
75: }
76: ```
77: 
78: ```tsx filename="app/ui/like-button.tsx" highlight={1} switcher
79: 'use client'
80: 
81: import { useState } from 'react'
82: 
83: export default function LikeButton({ likes }: { likes: number }) {
84:   // ...
85: }
86: ```
87: 
88: ```jsx filename="app/ui/like-button.js" highlight={1} switcher
89: 'use client'
90: 
91: import { useState } from 'react'
92: 
93: export default function LikeButton({ likes }) {
94:   // ...
95: }
96: ```
97: 
98: ## How do Server and Client Components work in Next.js?
99: 
100: ### On the server
101: 
102: On the server, Next.js uses React's APIs to orchestrate rendering. The rendering work is split into chunks, by individual route segments ([layouts and pages](/docs/app/getting-started/layouts-and-pages)), including [parallel route slots](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/parallel-routes) whether or not they are displayed:
103: 
104: - **Server Components** are rendered into a special data format called the React Server Component Payload (RSC Payload).
105: - **Client Components** and the RSC Payload are used to [prerender](/docs/app/glossary#prerendering) HTML.
106: 
107: > **What is the React Server Component Payload (RSC)?**
108: >
109: > The RSC Payload is a compact binary representation of the rendered React Server Components tree. It's used by React on the client to update the browser's DOM. The RSC Payload contains:
110: >
111: > - The rendered result of Server Components
112: > - Placeholders for where Client Components should be rendered and references to their JavaScript files
113: > - Any props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component
114: 
115: ### On the client (first load)
116: 
117: Then, on the client:
118: 
119: 1. **HTML** is used to immediately show a fast non-interactive preview of the route to the user.
120: 2. **RSC Payload** is used to reconcile the Client and Server Component trees.
121: 3. **JavaScript** is used to hydrate Client Components and make the application interactive.
122: 
123: > **What is hydration?**
124: >
125: > Hydration is React's process for attaching [event handlers](https://react.dev/learn/responding-to-events) to the DOM, to make the static HTML interactive.
126: 
127: ### Subsequent Navigations
128: 
129: On subsequent navigations:
130: 
131: - The **RSC Payload** is prefetched and cached for instant navigation.
132: - **Client Components** are rendered entirely on the client, without the server-rendered HTML.
133: 
134: ## Examples
135: 
136: ### Using Client Components
137: 
138: You can create a Client Component by adding the [`"use client"`](https://react.dev/reference/react/use-client) directive at the top of the file, above your imports.
139: 
140: ```tsx filename="app/ui/counter.tsx" highlight={1} switcher
141: 'use client'
142: 
143: import { useState } from 'react'
144: 
145: export default function Counter() {
146:   const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
147: 
148:   return (
149:     <div>
150:       <p>{count} likes</p>
151:       <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Click me</button>
152:     </div>
153:   )
154: }
155: ```
156: 
157: ```jsx filename="app/ui/counter.js" highlight={1} switcher
158: 'use client'
159: 
160: import { useState } from 'react'
161: 
162: export default function Counter() {
163:   const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
164: 
165:   return (
166:     <div>
167:       <p>{count} likes</p>
168:       <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Click me</button>
169:     </div>
170:   )
171: }
172: ```
173: 
174: `"use client"` is used to declare a **boundary** between the Server and Client module graphs (trees).
175: 
176: Once a file is marked with `"use client"`, **all of its imports and the components it directly renders are included in the client bundle**. This means you don’t need to add the directive to every component that is intended for the client.
177: 
178: This behavior applies to components that are part of the Client Component’s [module graph](/docs/app/glossary#module-graph), which includes the modules it imports and the components it renders directly. It does not apply to Server Components passed as children or other props. Those components are not imported into the Client Component’s module graph. They are rendered on the server and passed to the Client Component as rendered output.
179: 
180: See [Interleaving Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#interleaving-server-and-client-components) for how Server and Client Components can be combined.
181: 
182: ### Reducing JS bundle size
183: 
184: To reduce the size of your client JavaScript bundles, add `'use client'` to specific interactive components instead of marking large parts of your UI as Client Components.
185: 
186: For example, the `<Layout>` component contains mostly static elements like a logo and navigation links, but includes an interactive search bar. `<Search />` is interactive and needs to be a Client Component, however, the rest of the layout can remain a Server Component.
187: 
188: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" highlight={12} switcher
189: // Client Component
190: import Search from './search'
191: // Server Component
192: import Logo from './logo'
193: 
194: // Layout is a Server Component by default
195: export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
196:   return (
197:     <>
198:       <nav>
199:         <Logo />
200:         <Search />
201:       </nav>
202:       <main>{children}</main>
203:     </>
204:   )
205: }
206: ```
207: 
208: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" highlight={12} switcher
209: // Client Component
210: import Search from './search'
211: // Server Component
212: import Logo from './logo'
213: 
214: // Layout is a Server Component by default
215: export default function Layout({ children }) {
216:   return (
217:     <>
218:       <nav>
219:         <Logo />
220:         <Search />
221:       </nav>
222:       <main>{children}</main>
223:     </>
224:   )
225: }
226: ```
227: 
228: ```tsx filename="app/ui/search.tsx" highlight={1} switcher
229: 'use client'
230: 
231: export default function Search() {
232:   // ...
233: }
234: ```
235: 
236: ```jsx filename="app/ui/search.js" highlight={1} switcher
237: 'use client'
238: 
239: export default function Search() {
240:   // ...
241: }
242: ```
243: 
244: ### Passing data from Server to Client Components
245: 
246: You can pass data from Server Components to Client Components using props.
247: 
248: ```tsx filename="app/[id]/page.tsx" highlight={1,12} switcher
249: import LikeButton from '@/app/ui/like-button'
250: import { getPost } from '@/lib/data'
251: 
252: export default async function Page({
253:   params,
254: }: {
255:   params: Promise<{ id: string }>
256: }) {
257:   const { id } = await params
258:   const post = await getPost(id)
259: 
260:   return <LikeButton likes={post.likes} />
261: }
262: ```
263: 
264: ```jsx filename="app/[id]/page.js" highlight={1,7} switcher
265: import LikeButton from '@/app/ui/like-button'
266: import { getPost } from '@/lib/data'
267: 
268: export default async function Page({ params }) {
269:   const post = await getPost(params.id)
270: 
271:   return <LikeButton likes={post.likes} />
272: }
273: ```
274: 
275: ```tsx filename="app/ui/like-button.tsx" highlight={1} switcher
276: 'use client'
277: 
278: export default function LikeButton({ likes }: { likes: number }) {
279:   // ...
280: }
281: ```
282: 
283: ```jsx filename="app/ui/like-button.js" highlight={1} switcher
284: 'use client'
285: 
286: export default function LikeButton({ likes }) {
287:   // ...
288: }
289: ```
290: 
291: Alternatively, you can stream data from a Server Component to a Client Component with the [`use` API](https://react.dev/reference/react/use). See an [example](/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data#streaming-data-with-the-use-api).
292: 
293: > **Good to know**: Props passed to Client Components need to be [serializable](https://react.dev/reference/react/use-server#serializable-parameters-and-return-values) by React.
294: 
295: ### Interleaving Server and Client Components
296: 
297: You can pass Server Components as a prop to a Client Component. This allows you to visually nest server-rendered UI within Client components.
298: 
299: A common pattern is to use `children` to create a _slot_ in a `<ClientComponent>`. For example, a `<Cart>` component that fetches data on the server, inside a `<Modal>` component that uses client state to toggle visibility.
300: 
301: ```tsx filename="app/ui/modal.tsx" switcher
302: 'use client'
303: 
304: export default function Modal({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
305:   return <div>{children}</div>
306: }
307: ```
308: 
309: ```jsx filename="app/ui/modal.js" switcher
310: 'use client'
311: 
312: export default function Modal({ children }) {
313:   return <div>{children}</div>
314: }
315: ```
316: 
317: Then, in a parent Server Component (e.g.`<Page>`), you can pass a `<Cart>` as the child of the `<Modal>`:
318: 
319: ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx"  highlight={7} switcher
320: import Modal from './ui/modal'
321: import Cart from './ui/cart'
322: 
323: export default function Page() {
324:   return (
325:     <Modal>
326:       <Cart />
327:     </Modal>
328:   )
329: }
330: ```
331: 
332: ```jsx filename="app/page.js" highlight={7} switcher
333: import Modal from './ui/modal'
334: import Cart from './ui/cart'
335: 
336: export default function Page() {
337:   return (
338:     <Modal>
339:       <Cart />
340:     </Modal>
341:   )
342: }
343: ```
344: 
345: In this pattern, Server Components are rendered on the server ahead of time, even when passed as props to Client Components. The React Server Component Payload contains the rendered result of those Server Components, plus placeholders for where Client Components should be rendered and references to their JavaScript files.
346: 
347: ### Context providers
348: 
349: [React context](https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context) is commonly used to share global state like the current theme. However, React context is not supported in Server Components.
350: 
351: To use context, create a Client Component that accepts `children`:
352: 
353: ```tsx filename="app/theme-provider.tsx" switcher
354: 'use client'
355: 
356: import { createContext } from 'react'
357: 
358: export const ThemeContext = createContext({})
359: 
360: export default function ThemeProvider({
361:   children,
362: }: {
363:   children: React.ReactNode
364: }) {
365:   return <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>
366: }
367: ```
368: 
369: ```jsx filename="app/theme-provider.js" switcher
370: 'use client'
371: 
372: import { createContext } from 'react'
373: 
374: export const ThemeContext = createContext({})
375: 
376: export default function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
377:   return <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>
378: }
379: ```
380: 
381: Then, import it into a Server Component (e.g. `layout`):
382: 
383: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
384: import ThemeProvider from './theme-provider'
385: 
386: export default function RootLayout({
387:   children,
388: }: {
389:   children: React.ReactNode
390: }) {
391:   return (
392:     <html>
393:       <body>
394:         <ThemeProvider>{children}</ThemeProvider>
395:       </body>
396:     </html>
397:   )
398: }
399: ```
400: 
401: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
402: import ThemeProvider from './theme-provider'
403: 
404: export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
405:   return (
406:     <html>
407:       <body>
408:         <ThemeProvider>{children}</ThemeProvider>
409:       </body>
410:     </html>
411:   )
412: }
413: ```
414: 
415: Your Server Component will now be able to directly render your provider, and all other Client Components throughout your app will be able to consume this context.
416: 
417: > **Good to know**: You should render providers as deep as possible in the tree – notice how `ThemeProvider` only wraps `{children}` instead of the entire `<html>` document. This makes it easier for Next.js to optimize the static parts of your Server Components.
418: 
419: To pass server-fetched data through context and read it in Client Components with `use()`, see [Using React's `use` within a Context Provider](/docs/app/guides/single-page-applications#using-reacts-use-within-a-context-provider).
420: 
421: ### Third-party components
422: 
423: When using a third-party component that relies on client-only features, you can wrap it in a Client Component to ensure it works as expected.
424: 
425: For example, the `<Carousel />` can be imported from the `acme-carousel` package. This component uses `useState`, but it doesn't yet have the `"use client"` directive.
426: 
427: If you use `<Carousel />` within a Client Component, it will work as expected:
428: 
429: ```tsx filename="app/gallery.tsx" switcher
430: 'use client'
431: 
432: import { useState } from 'react'
433: import { Carousel } from 'acme-carousel'
434: 
435: export default function Gallery() {
436:   const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false)
437: 
438:   return (
439:     <div>
440:       <button onClick={() => setIsOpen(true)}>View pictures</button>
441:       {/* Works, since Carousel is used within a Client Component */}
442:       {isOpen && <Carousel />}
443:     </div>
444:   )
445: }
446: ```
447: 
448: ```jsx filename="app/gallery.js" switcher
449: 'use client'
450: 
451: import { useState } from 'react'
452: import { Carousel } from 'acme-carousel'
453: 
454: export default function Gallery() {
455:   const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false)
456: 
457:   return (
458:     <div>
459:       <button onClick={() => setIsOpen(true)}>View pictures</button>
460:       {/*  Works, since Carousel is used within a Client Component */}
461:       {isOpen && <Carousel />}
462:     </div>
463:   )
464: }
465: ```
466: 
467: However, if you try to use it directly within a Server Component, you'll see an error. This is because Next.js doesn't know `<Carousel />` is using client-only features.
468: 
469: To fix this, you can wrap third-party components that rely on client-only features in your own Client Components:
470: 
471: ```tsx filename="app/carousel.tsx" switcher
472: 'use client'
473: 
474: import { Carousel } from 'acme-carousel'
475: 
476: export default Carousel
477: ```
478: 
479: ```jsx filename="app/carousel.js" switcher
480: 'use client'
481: 
482: import { Carousel } from 'acme-carousel'
483: 
484: export default Carousel
485: ```
486: 
487: Now, you can use `<Carousel />` directly within a Server Component:
488: 
489: ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
490: import Carousel from './carousel'
491: 
492: export default function Page() {
493:   return (
494:     <div>
495:       <p>View pictures</p>
496:       {/*  Works, since Carousel is a Client Component */}
497:       <Carousel />
498:     </div>
499:   )
500: }
501: ```
502: 
503: ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
504: import Carousel from './carousel'
505: 
506: export default function Page() {
507:   return (
508:     <div>
509:       <p>View pictures</p>
510:       {/*  Works, since Carousel is a Client Component */}
511:       <Carousel />
512:     </div>
513:   )
514: }
515: ```
516: 
517: > **Advice for Library Authors**
518: >
519: > If you’re building a component library, add the `"use client"` directive to entry points that rely on client-only features. This lets your users import components into Server Components without needing to create wrappers.
520: >
521: > It's worth noting some bundlers might strip out `"use client"` directives. You can find an example of how to configure esbuild to include the `"use client"` directive in the [React Wrap Balancer](https://github.com/shuding/react-wrap-balancer/blob/main/tsup.config.ts#L10-L13) and [Vercel Analytics](https://github.com/vercel/analytics/blob/main/packages/web/tsup.config.js#L26-L30) repositories.
522: 
523: ### Preventing environment poisoning
524: 
525: JavaScript modules can be shared between both Server and Client Components modules. This means it's possible to accidentally import server-only code into the client. For example, consider the following function:
526: 
527: ```ts filename="lib/data.ts" switcher
528: export async function getData() {
529:   const res = await fetch('https://external-service.com/data', {
530:     headers: {
531:       authorization: process.env.API_KEY,
532:     },
533:   })
534: 
535:   return res.json()
536: }
537: ```
538: 
539: ```js filename="lib/data.js" switcher
540: export async function getData() {
541:   const res = await fetch('https://external-service.com/data', {
542:     headers: {
543:       authorization: process.env.API_KEY,
544:     },
545:   })
546: 
547:   return res.json()
548: }
549: ```
550: 
551: This function contains an `API_KEY` that should never be exposed to the client.
552: 
553: In Next.js, only environment variables prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` are included in the client bundle. If variables are not prefixed, Next.js replaces them with an empty string.
554: 
555: As a result, even though `getData()` can be imported and executed on the client, it won't work as expected.
556: 
557: To prevent accidental usage in Client Components, you can use the [`server-only` package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/server-only).
558: 
559: Then, import the package into a file that contains server-only code:
560: 
561: ```js filename="lib/data.js"
562: import 'server-only'
563: 
564: export async function getData() {
565:   const res = await fetch('https://external-service.com/data', {
566:     headers: {
567:       authorization: process.env.API_KEY,
568:     },
569:   })
570: 
571:   return res.json()
572: }
573: ```
574: 
575: Now, if you try to import the module into a Client Component, there will be a build-time error.
576: 
577: The corresponding [`client-only` package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/client-only) can be used to mark modules that contain client-only logic like code that accesses the `window` object.
578: 
579: In Next.js, installing `server-only` or `client-only` is **optional**. However, if your linting rules flag extraneous dependencies, you may install them to avoid issues.
580: 
581: ```bash package="npm"
582: npm install server-only
583: ```
584: 
585: ```bash package="yarn"
586: yarn add server-only
587: ```
588: 
589: ```bash package="pnpm"
590: pnpm add server-only
591: ```
592: 
593: ```bash package="bun"
594: bun add server-only
595: ```
596: 
597: Next.js handles `server-only` and `client-only` imports internally to provide clearer error messages when a module is used in the wrong environment. The contents of these packages from NPM are not used by Next.js.
598: 
599: Next.js also provides its own type declarations for `server-only` and `client-only`, for TypeScript configurations where [`noUncheckedSideEffectImports`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#noUncheckedSideEffectImports) is active.

(End of file - total 599 lines)
</content>

2: title: Fetching Data

15: 
16: This page will walk you through how you can fetch data in [Server](#server-components) and [Client](#client-components) Components, and how to [stream](#streaming) components that depend on uncached data.
17: 
18: ## Fetching data
19: 
20: ### Server Components
21: 
22: You can fetch data in Server Components using any asynchronous I/O, such as:
23: 
24: 1. The [`fetch` API](#with-the-fetch-api)
25: 2. An [ORM or database](#with-an-orm-or-database)
26: 
27: #### With the `fetch` API
28: 
29: To fetch data with the `fetch` API, turn your component into an asynchronous function, and await the `fetch` call. For example:
30: 
31: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" switcher
32: export default async function Page() {
33:   const data = await fetch('https://api.vercel.app/blog')
34:   const posts = await data.json()
35:   return (
36:     <ul>
37:       {posts.map((post) => (
38:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
39:       ))}
40:     </ul>
41:   )
42: }
43: ```
44: 
45: ```jsx filename="app/blog/page.js" switcher
46: export default async function Page() {
47:   const data = await fetch('https://api.vercel.app/blog')
48:   const posts = await data.json()
49:   return (
50:     <ul>
51:       {posts.map((post) => (
52:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
53:       ))}
54:     </ul>
55:   )
56: }
57: ```
58: 
59: > **Good to know:**
60: >
61: > - Identical `fetch` requests in a React component tree are [memoized](/docs/app/glossary#memoization) by default, so you can fetch data in the component that needs it instead of drilling props.
62: > - `fetch` requests are not cached by default and will block the page from rendering until the request is complete. Use the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive to cache results, or wrap the fetching component in [`<Suspense>`](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#streaming-uncached-data) to stream fresh data at request time. See [caching](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) for details.
63: > - During development, you can log `fetch` calls for better visibility and debugging. See the [`logging` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/logging).
64: 
65: #### With an ORM or database
66: 
67: Since Server Components are rendered on the server, credentials and query logic will not be included in the client bundle so you can safely make database queries using an ORM or database client.
68: 
69: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" switcher
70: import { db, posts } from '@/lib/db'
71: 
72: export default async function Page() {
73:   const allPosts = await db.select().from(posts)
74:   return (
75:     <ul>
76:       {allPosts.map((post) => (
77:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
78:       ))}
79:     </ul>
80:   )
81: }
82: ```
83: 
84: ```jsx filename="app/blog/page.js" switcher
85: import { db, posts } from '@/lib/db'
86: 
87: export default async function Page() {
88:   const allPosts = await db.select().from(posts)
89:   return (
90:     <ul>
91:       {allPosts.map((post) => (
92:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
93:       ))}
94:     </ul>
95:   )
96: }
97: ```
98: 
99: You should still ensure requests are properly authenticated and authorized. For best practices on securing server-side data access, see the [data security guide](/docs/app/guides/data-security).
100: 
101: ### Streaming
102: 
103: When you fetch data in Server Components, the data is fetched and rendered on the server for each request. If you have any slow data requests, the whole route will be blocked from rendering until all the data is fetched.
104: 
105: To improve the initial load time and user experience, you can break the page into smaller _chunks_ and progressively send those chunks from the server to the client. This is called streaming. See the [Streaming guide](/docs/app/guides/streaming) for a deeper look at how streaming works, including the HTTP contract, infrastructure considerations, and performance trade-offs.
106: 
107: <Image
108:   alt="How Server Rendering with Streaming Works"
109:   srcLight="/docs/light/server-rendering-with-streaming.png"
110:   srcDark="/docs/dark/server-rendering-with-streaming.png"
111:   width="1600"
112:   height="785"
113: />
114: 
115: There are two ways you can use streaming in your application:
116: 
117: 1. Wrapping a page with a [`loading.js` file](#with-loadingjs)
118: 2. Wrapping a component with [`<Suspense>`](#with-suspense)
119: 
120: > **Good to know:** Bots and crawlers are served differently from browsers. Next.js waits for data fetching to finish and sends the fully rendered page instead of streaming it progressively. See [Bots and crawlers](/docs/app/guides/streaming#bots-and-crawlers).
121: 
122: #### With `loading.js`
123: 
124: You can create a `loading.js` file in the same folder as your page to stream the **entire page** while the data is being fetched. For example, to stream `app/blog/page.js`, add the file inside the `app/blog` folder.
125: 
126: <Image
127:   alt="Blog folder structure with loading.js file"
128:   srcLight="/docs/light/loading-file.png"
129:   srcDark="/docs/dark/loading-file.png"
130:   width="1600"
131:   height="525"
132: />
133: 
134: ```tsx filename="app/blog/loading.tsx" switcher
135: export default function Loading() {
136:   // Define the Loading UI here
137:   return <div>Loading...</div>
138: }
139: ```
140: 
141: ```jsx filename="app/blog/loading.js" switcher
142: export default function Loading() {
143:   // Define the Loading UI here
144:   return <div>Loading...</div>
145: }
146: ```
147: 
148: On navigation, the user will immediately see the layout and a [loading state](#creating-meaningful-loading-states) while the page is being rendered. The new content will then be automatically swapped in once rendering is complete.
149: 
150: <Image
151:   alt="Loading UI"
152:   srcLight="/docs/light/loading-ui.png"
153:   srcDark="/docs/dark/loading-ui.png"
154:   width="1600"
155:   height="691"
156: />
157: 
158: Behind the scenes, `loading.js` will be [nested inside `layout.js`](/docs/app/getting-started/project-structure#component-hierarchy), and will automatically wrap the `page.js` file and any children below in a `<Suspense>` boundary.
159: 
160: <Image
161:   alt="loading.js overview"
162:   srcLight="/docs/light/loading-overview.png"
163:   srcDark="/docs/dark/loading-overview.png"
164:   width="1600"
165:   height="768"
166: />
167: 
168: Because of this, a layout that accesses uncached or runtime data (e.g. `cookies()`, `headers()`, or uncached fetches) does not fall back to a same route segment `loading.js`. Instead, it blocks navigation until the layout finishes rendering. [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) prevents this by guiding you with a build-time error.
169: 
170: To fix this, wrap the uncached access in its own [`<Suspense>`](#with-suspense) boundary with a fallback, or move the data fetching into `page.js` where `loading.js` can cover it. See [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) for more details.
171: 
172: This is why, while `loading.js` works well for streaming route segments, using `<Suspense>` closer to the runtime or uncached data access is recommended.
173: 
174: #### With `<Suspense>`
175: 
176: `<Suspense>` allows you to be more granular about what parts of the page to stream. For example, you can immediately show any page content that falls outside of the `<Suspense>` boundary, and stream in the list of blog posts inside the boundary.
177: 
178: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" switcher
179: import { Suspense } from 'react'
180: import BlogList from '@/components/BlogList'
181: import BlogListSkeleton from '@/components/BlogListSkeleton'
182: 
183: export default function BlogPage() {
184:   return (
185:     <div>
186:       {/* This content will be sent to the client immediately */}
187:       <header>
188:         <h1>Welcome to the Blog</h1>
189:         <p>Read the latest posts below.</p>
190:       </header>
191:       <main>
192:         {/* If there's any dynamic content inside this boundary, it will be streamed in */}
193:         <Suspense fallback={<BlogListSkeleton />}>
194:           <BlogList />
195:         </Suspense>
196:       </main>
197:     </div>
198:   )
199: }
200: ```
201: 
202: ```jsx filename="app/blog/page.js" switcher
203: import { Suspense } from 'react'
204: import BlogList from '@/components/BlogList'
205: import BlogListSkeleton from '@/components/BlogListSkeleton'
206: 
207: export default function BlogPage() {
208:   return (
209:     <div>
210:       {/* This content will be sent to the client immediately */}
211:       <header>
212:         <h1>Welcome to the Blog</h1>
213:         <p>Read the latest posts below.</p>
214:       </header>
215:       <main>
216:         {/* If there's any dynamic content inside this boundary, it will be streamed in */}
217:         <Suspense fallback={<BlogListSkeleton />}>
218:           <BlogList />
219:         </Suspense>
220:       </main>
221:     </div>
222:   )
223: }
224: ```
225: 
226: #### Creating meaningful loading states
227: 
228: An instant loading state is fallback UI that is shown immediately to the user after navigation. For the best user experience, we recommend designing loading states that are meaningful and help users understand the app is responding. For example, you can use skeletons and spinners, or a small but meaningful part of future screens such as a cover photo, title, etc.
229: 
230: In development, you can preview and inspect the loading state of your components using the [React Devtools](https://react.dev/learn/react-developer-tools).
231: 
232: ### Client Components
233: 
234: There are two ways to fetch data in Client Components, using:
235: 
236: 1. React's [`use` API](https://react.dev/reference/react/use)
237: 2. A community library like [SWR](https://swr.vercel.app/) or [React Query](https://tanstack.com/query/latest)
238: 
239: #### Streaming data with the `use` API
240: 
241: You can use React's [`use` API](https://react.dev/reference/react/use) to [stream](#streaming) data from the server to client. Start by fetching data in your Server component, and pass the promise to your Client Component as prop:
242: 
243: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" switcher
244: import Posts from '@/app/ui/posts'
245: import { Suspense } from 'react'
246: 
247: export default function Page() {
248:   // Don't await the data fetching function
249:   const posts = getPosts()
250: 
251:   return (
252:     <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
253:       <Posts posts={posts} />
254:     </Suspense>
255:   )
256: }
257: ```
258: 
259: ```jsx filename="app/blog/page.js" switcher
260: import Posts from '@/app/ui/posts'
261: import { Suspense } from 'react'
262: 
263: export default function Page() {
264:   // Don't await the data fetching function
265:   const posts = getPosts()
266: 
267:   return (
268:     <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
269:       <Posts posts={posts} />
270:     </Suspense>
271:   )
272: }
273: ```
274: 
275: Then, in your Client Component, use the `use` API to read the promise:
276: 
277: ```tsx filename="app/ui/posts.tsx" switcher
278: 'use client'
279: import { use } from 'react'
280: 
281: export default function Posts({
282:   posts,
283: }: {
284:   posts: Promise<{ id: string; title: string }[]>
285: }) {
286:   const allPosts = use(posts)
287: 
288:   return (
289:     <ul>
290:       {allPosts.map((post) => (
291:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
292:       ))}
293:     </ul>
294:   )
295: }
296: ```
297: 
298: ```jsx filename="app/ui/posts.js" switcher
299: 'use client'
300: import { use } from 'react'
301: 
302: export default function Posts({ posts }) {
303:   const allPosts = use(posts)
304: 
305:   return (
306:     <ul>
307:       {allPosts.map((post) => (
308:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
309:       ))}
310:     </ul>
311:   )
312: }
313: ```
314: 
315: In the example above, the `<Posts>` component is wrapped in a [`<Suspense>` boundary](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense). This means the fallback will be shown while the promise is being resolved. Learn more about [streaming](#streaming).
316: 
317: You can resolve a promise on the server with `await` or in a Client Component with `use()`. React covers [when to resolve a Promise in a Server or Client Component](https://react.dev/reference/react/use#resolve-promise-in-server-or-client-component). To share one promise with many Client Components instead of passing it as a prop, provide it through context. See [Using React's `use` within a Context Provider](/docs/app/guides/single-page-applications#using-reacts-use-within-a-context-provider).
318: 
319: #### Community libraries
320: 
321: You can use a community library like [SWR](https://swr.vercel.app/) or [React Query](https://tanstack.com/query/latest) to fetch data in Client Components. These libraries have their own semantics for caching, streaming, and other features. For example, with SWR:
322: 
323: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" switcher
324: 'use client'
325: import useSWR from 'swr'
326: 
327: const fetcher = (url) => fetch(url).then((r) => r.json())
328: 
329: export default function BlogPage() {
330:   const { data, error, isLoading } = useSWR(
331:     'https://api.vercel.app/blog',
332:     fetcher
333:   )
334: 
335:   if (isLoading) return <div>Loading...</div>
336:   if (error) return <div>Error: {error.message}</div>
337: 
338:   return (
339:     <ul>
340:       {data.map((post: { id: string; title: string }) => (
341:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
342:       ))}
343:     </ul>
344:   )
345: }
346: ```
347: 
348: ```jsx filename="app/blog/page.js" switcher
349: 'use client'
350: 
351: import useSWR from 'swr'
352: 
353: const fetcher = (url) => fetch(url).then((r) => r.json())
354: 
355: export default function BlogPage() {
356:   const { data, error, isLoading } = useSWR(
357:     'https://api.vercel.app/blog',
358:     fetcher
359:   )
360: 
361:   if (isLoading) return <div>Loading...</div>
362:   if (error) return <div>Error: {error.message}</div>
363: 
364:   return (
365:     <ul>
366:       {data.map((post) => (
367:         <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>
368:       ))}
369:     </ul>
370:   )
371: }
372: ```
373: 
374: ## Examples
375: 
376: ### Sequential data fetching
377: 
378: Sequential data fetching happens when one request depends on data from another.
379: 
380: For example, `<Playlists>` can only fetch data after `getArtist()` resolves because it needs the `artistID`:
381: 
382: ```tsx filename="app/artist/[username]/page.tsx" switcher
383: export default async function Page({
384:   params,
385: }: {
386:   params: Promise<{ username: string }>
387: }) {
388:   const { username } = await params
389:   // Get artist information
390:   const artist = await getArtist(username)
391: 
392:   return (
393:     <>
394:       <h1>{artist.name}</h1>
395:       {/* Show fallback UI while the Playlists component is loading */}
396:       <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
397:         {/* Pass the artist ID to the Playlists component */}
398:         <Playlists artistID={artist.id} />
399:       </Suspense>
400:     </>
401:   )
402: }
403: 
404: async function Playlists({ artistID }: { artistID: string }) {
405:   // Use the artist ID to fetch playlists
406:   const playlists = await getArtistPlaylists(artistID)
407: 
408:   return (
409:     <ul>
410:       {playlists.map((playlist) => (
411:         <li key={playlist.id}>{playlist.name}</li>
412:       ))}
413:     </ul>
414:   )
415: }
416: ```
417: 
418: ```jsx filename="app/artist/[username]/page.js" switcher
419: export default async function Page({ params }) {
420:   const { username } = await params
421:   // Get artist information
422:   const artist = await getArtist(username)
423: 
424:   return (
425:     <>
426:       <h1>{artist.name}</h1>
427:       {/* Show fallback UI while the Playlists component is loading */}
428:       <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
429:         {/* Pass the artist ID to the Playlists component */}
430:         <Playlists artistID={artist.id} />
431:       </Suspense>
432:     </>
433:   )
434: }
435: 
436: async function Playlists({ artistID }) {
437:   // Use the artist ID to fetch playlists
438:   const playlists = await getArtistPlaylists(artistID)
439: 
440:   return (
441:     <ul>
442:       {playlists.map((playlist) => (
443:         <li key={playlist.id}>{playlist.name}</li>
444:       ))}
445:     </ul>
446:   )
447: }
448: ```
449: 
450: In this example, `<Suspense>` allows the playlists to stream in after the artist data loads. However, the page still waits for the artist data before displaying anything. To prevent this, you can wrap the entire page component in a `<Suspense>` boundary (for example, using a [`loading.js` file](#with-loadingjs)) to show a loading state immediately.
451: 
452: Ensure your data source can resolve the first request quickly, as it blocks everything else. If you can't optimize the request further, consider [caching](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) the result if the data changes infrequently.
453: 
454: ### Parallel data fetching
455: 
456: Parallel data fetching happens when data requests in a route are eagerly initiated and start at the same time.
457: 
458: By default, [layouts and pages](/docs/app/getting-started/layouts-and-pages) are rendered in parallel. So each segment starts fetching data as soon as possible.
459: 
460: However, within _any_ component, multiple `async`/`await` requests can still be sequential if placed after the other. For example, `getAlbums` will be blocked until `getArtist` is resolved:
461: 
462: ```tsx filename="app/artist/[username]/page.tsx" switcher
463: import { getArtist, getAlbums } from '@/app/lib/data'
464: 
465: export default async function Page({ params }) {
466:   // These requests will be sequential
467:   const { username } = await params
468:   const artist = await getArtist(username)
469:   const albums = await getAlbums(username)
470:   return <div>{artist.name}</div>
471: }
472: ```
473: 
474: Start multiple requests by calling `fetch`, then await them with [`Promise.all`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all). Requests begin as soon as `fetch` is called.
475: 
476: ```tsx filename="app/artist/[username]/page.tsx" highlight={3,8,24} switcher
477: import Albums from './albums'
478: 
479: async function getArtist(username: string) {
480:   const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/artist/${username}`)
481:   return res.json()
482: }
483: 
484: async function getAlbums(username: string) {
485:   const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/artist/${username}/albums`)
486:   return res.json()
487: }
488: 
489: export default async function Page({
490:   params,
491: }: {
492:   params: Promise<{ username: string }>
493: }) {
494:   const { username } = await params
495: 
496:   // Initiate requests
497:   const artistData = getArtist(username)
498:   const albumsData = getAlbums(username)
499: 
500:   const [artist, albums] = await Promise.all([artistData, albumsData])
501: 
502:   return (
503:     <>
504:       <h1>{artist.name}</h1>
505:       <Albums list={albums} />
506:     </>
507:   )
508: }
509: ```
510: 
511: ```jsx filename="app/artist/[username]/page.js" highlight={3,8,20} switcher
512: import Albums from './albums'
513: 
514: async function getArtist(username) {
515:   const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/artist/${username}`)
516:   return res.json()
517: }
518: 
519: async function getAlbums(username) {
520:   const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/artist/${username}/albums`)
521:   return res.json()
522: }
523: 
524: export default async function Page({ params }) {
525:   const { username } = await params
526: 
527:   // Initiate requests
528:   const artistData = getArtist(username)
529:   const albumsData = getAlbums(username)
530: 
531:   const [artist, albums] = await Promise.all([artistData, albumsData])
532: 
533:   return (
534:     <>
535:       <h1>{artist.name}</h1>
536:       <Albums list={albums} />
537:     </>
538:   )
539: }
540: ```
541: 
542: > **Good to know:** If one request fails when using `Promise.all`, the entire operation will fail. To handle this, you can use the [`Promise.allSettled`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/allSettled) method instead.
543: 
544: ### Reusing data with `React.cache`
545: 
546: Wrap a data-fetching function in [`React.cache`](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) so multiple components in the same request share one result instead of refetching:
547: 
548: ```ts filename="app/lib/user.ts" switcher
549: import { cache } from 'react'
550: 
551: export const getUser = cache(async () => {
552:   const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/user')
553:   return res.json()
554: })
555: ```
556: 
557: ```js filename="app/lib/user.js" switcher
558: import { cache } from 'react'
559: 
560: export const getUser = cache(async () => {
561:   const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/user')
562:   return res.json()
563: })
564: ```
565: 
566: Server Components can call `getUser()` directly:
567: 
568: ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/page.tsx" switcher
569: import { getUser } from '../lib/user'
570: 
571: export default async function DashboardPage() {
572:   const user = await getUser() // Cached - same request, no duplicate fetch
573:   return <h1>Dashboard for {user.name}</h1>
574: }
575: ```
576: 
577: ```jsx filename="app/dashboard/page.js" switcher
578: import { getUser } from '../lib/user'
579: 
580: export default async function DashboardPage() {
581:   const user = await getUser() // Cached - same request, no duplicate fetch
582:   return <h1>Dashboard for {user.name}</h1>
583: }
584: ```
585: 
586: Since `getUser` is wrapped with `React.cache`, multiple calls within the same request return the same memoized result, whether called directly in Server Components or resolved via context in Client Components.
587: 
588: > **Good to know**: `React.cache` is scoped to the current request only. Each request gets its own memoization scope with no sharing between requests.

(End of file - total 588 lines)
</content>

1: ---
2: title: Route Handlers
3: nav_title: Route Handlers
4: description: Learn how to use Route Handlers
5: related:
6:   title: API Reference
7:   description: Learn more about Route Handlers
8:   links:
9:     - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route
10:     - app/guides/backend-for-frontend
11: ---
12: 
13: ## Route Handlers
14: 
15: Route Handlers allow you to create custom request handlers for a given route using the Web [Request](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) and [Response](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response) APIs.
16: 
17: <Image
18:   alt="Route.js Special File"
19:   srcLight="/docs/light/route-special-file.png"
20:   srcDark="/docs/dark/route-special-file.png"
21:   width="1600"
22:   height="444"
23: />
24: 
25: > **Good to know**: Route Handlers are only available inside the `app` directory. They are the equivalent of [API Routes](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/api-routes) inside the `pages` directory meaning you **do not** need to use API Routes and Route Handlers together.
26: 
27: ### Convention
28: 
29: Route Handlers are defined in a [`route.js|ts` file](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) inside the `app` directory:
30: 
31: ```ts filename="app/api/route.ts" switcher
32: export async function GET(request: Request) {}
33: ```
34: 
35: ```js filename="app/api/route.js" switcher
36: export async function GET(request) {}
37: ```
38: 
39: Route Handlers can be nested anywhere inside the `app` directory, similar to `page.js` and `layout.js`. But there **cannot** be a `route.js` file at the same route segment level as `page.js`.
40: 
41: ### Supported HTTP Methods
42: 
43: The following [HTTP methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods) are supported: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS`. If an unsupported method is called, Next.js will return a `405 Method Not Allowed` response.
44: 
45: ### Extended `NextRequest` and `NextResponse` APIs
46: 
47: In addition to supporting the native [Request](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) and [Response](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response) APIs, Next.js extends them with [`NextRequest`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-request) and [`NextResponse`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response) to provide convenient helpers for advanced use cases.
48: 
49: ### Caching
50: 
51: Route Handlers are not cached by default. You can, however, opt into caching for `GET` methods. Other supported HTTP methods are **not** cached. To cache a `GET` method, use a [route config option](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components#dynamic) such as `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` in your Route Handler file.
52: 
53: ```ts filename="app/items/route.ts" switcher
54: export const dynamic = 'force-static'
55: 
56: export async function GET() {
57:   const res = await fetch('https://data.mongodb-api.com/...', {
58:     headers: {
59:       'Content-Type': 'application/json',
60:       'API-Key': process.env.DATA_API_KEY,
61:     },
62:   })
63:   const data = await res.json()
64: 
65:   return Response.json({ data })
66: }
67: ```
68: 
69: ```js filename="app/items/route.js" switcher
70: export const dynamic = 'force-static'
71: 
72: export async function GET() {
73:   const res = await fetch('https://data.mongodb-api.com/...', {
74:     headers: {
75:       'Content-Type': 'application/json',
76:       'API-Key': process.env.DATA_API_KEY,
77:     },
78:   })
79:   const data = await res.json()
80: 
81:   return Response.json({ data })
82: }
83: ```
84: 
85: > **Good to know**: Other supported HTTP methods are **not** cached, even if they are placed alongside a `GET` method that is cached, in the same file.
86: 
87: #### With Cache Components
88: 
89: When [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) is enabled, `GET` Route Handlers follow the same model as normal UI routes in your application. They run at request time by default, can be prerendered when they don't access uncached or runtime data, and you can use `use cache` to include uncached data in the static response.
90: 
91: **Static example** - doesn't access uncached or runtime data, so it will be prerendered at build time:
92: 
93: ```tsx filename="app/api/project-info/route.ts"
94: export async function GET() {
95:   return Response.json({
96:     projectName: 'Next.js',
97:   })
98: }
99: ```
100: 
101: **Dynamic example** - accesses non-deterministic operations. During the build, prerendering stops when `Math.random()` is called, deferring to request-time rendering:
102: 
103: ```tsx filename="app/api/random-number/route.ts"
104: export async function GET() {
105:   return Response.json({
106:     randomNumber: Math.random(),
107:   })
108: }
109: ```
110: 
111: **Runtime data example** - accesses request-specific data. Prerendering terminates when runtime APIs like `headers()` are called:
112: 
113: ```tsx filename="app/api/user-agent/route.ts"
114: import { headers } from 'next/headers'
115: 
116: export async function GET() {
117:   const headersList = await headers()
118:   const userAgent = headersList.get('user-agent')
119: 
120:   return Response.json({ userAgent })
121: }
122: ```
123: 
124: > **Good to know**: Prerendering stops if the `GET` handler accesses network requests, database queries, async file system operations, request object properties (like `req.url`, `request.headers`, `request.cookies`, `request.body`), runtime APIs like [`cookies()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies), [`headers()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers), [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection), or non-deterministic operations.
125: 
126: **Cached example** - accesses uncached data (database query) but caches it with `use cache`, allowing it to be included in the prerendered response:
127: 
128: ```tsx filename="app/api/products/route.ts"
129: import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'
130: 
131: export async function GET() {
132:   const products = await getProducts()
133:   return Response.json(products)
134: }
135: 
136: async function getProducts() {
137:   'use cache'
138:   cacheLife('hours')
139: 
140:   return await db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
141: }
142: ```
143: 
144: > **Good to know**: `use cache` cannot be used directly inside a Route Handler body; extract it to a helper function. Cached responses revalidate according to `cacheLife` when a new request arrives.
145: 
146: ### Special Route Handlers
147: 
148: Special Route Handlers like [`sitemap.ts`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/sitemap), [`opengraph-image.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image), and [`icon.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons), and other [metadata files](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata) remain static by default unless they use Request-time APIs or dynamic config options.
149: 
150: ### Route Resolution
151: 
152: You can consider a `route` the lowest level routing primitive.
153: 
154: - They **do not** participate in layouts or client-side navigations like `page`.
155: - There **cannot** be a `route.js` file at the same route as `page.js`.
156: 
157: | Page                 | Route              | Result                       |
158: | -------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------- |
159: | `app/page.js`        | `app/route.js`     | <Cross size={18} /> Conflict |
160: | `app/page.js`        | `app/api/route.js` | <Check size={18} /> Valid    |
161: | `app/[user]/page.js` | `app/api/route.js` | <Check size={18} /> Valid    |
162: 
163: Each `route.js` or `page.js` file takes over all HTTP verbs for that route.
164: 
165: ```ts filename="app/page.ts" switcher
166: export default function Page() {
167:   return <h1>Hello, Next.js!</h1>
168: }
169: 
170: // Conflict
171: // `app/route.ts`
172: export async function POST(request: Request) {}
173: ```
174: 
175: ```js filename="app/page.js" switcher
176: export default function Page() {
177:   return <h1>Hello, Next.js!</h1>
178: }
179: 
180: // Conflict
181: // `app/route.js`
182: export async function POST(request) {}
183: ```
184: 
185: Read more about how Route Handlers [complement your frontend application](/docs/app/guides/backend-for-frontend), or explore the Route Handlers [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route).
186: 
187: ### Route Context Helper
188: 
189: In TypeScript, you can type the `context` parameter for Route Handlers with the globally available [`RouteContext`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route#route-context-helper) helper:
190: 
191: ```ts filename="app/users/[id]/route.ts" switcher
192: import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
193: 
194: export async function GET(_req: NextRequest, ctx: RouteContext<'/users/[id]'>) {
195:   const { id } = await ctx.params
196:   return Response.json({ id })
197: }
198: ```
199: 
200: > **Good to know**
201: >
202: > - Types are generated during `next dev`, `next build` or `next typegen`.

(End of file - total 202 lines)
</content>
```
