540: function DosageSection({ label }: { label: ProductLabel }) {
541:   const plainFragments = usefulFragments(label.dosageAndAdministration);
542:   const richFragments = usefulFragments(label.dosageAndAdministrationTable);

544:   if (plainFragments.length === 0 && richFragments.length === 0) {

576:                       </tr>
577:                     ))}
578:                   </tbody>
579:                 </table>

591:       })}

1: ---
2: title: generateMetadata
3: description: Learn how to add Metadata to your Next.js application for improved search engine optimization (SEO) and web shareability.
4: related:
5:   title: Next Steps
6:   description: View all the Metadata API options.
7:   links:
8:     - app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata

11:     - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents
12: ---
13: 
14: You can use the `metadata` object or the `generateMetadata` function to define metadata.
15: 
16: ## The `metadata` object
17: 
18: To define static metadata, export a [`Metadata` object](#metadata-fields) from a `layout.js` or `page.js` file.
19: 
20: ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx" switcher
21: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
22: 
23: export const metadata: Metadata = {
24:   title: '...',
25:   description: '...',
26: }
27: 
28: export default function Page() {}
29: ```
30: 
31: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js" switcher
32: export const metadata = {
33:   title: '...',
34:   description: '...',
35: }
36: 
37: export default function Page() {}
38: ```
39: 
40: > See the [Metadata Fields](#metadata-fields) for a complete list of supported options.
41: 
42: ## `generateMetadata` function
43: 
44: Dynamic metadata depends on **dynamic information**, such as the current route parameters, external data, or `metadata` in parent segments, can be set by exporting a `generateMetadata` function that returns a [`Metadata` object](#metadata-fields).
45: 
46: Resolving `generateMetadata` is part of rendering the page. If the page can be prerendered and `generateMetadata` doesn't introduce dynamic behavior, the resulting metadata is included in the page's initial HTML.
47: 
48: Otherwise the metadata resolved from `generateMetadata` [can be streamed](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#streaming-metadata) after sending the initial UI.
49: 
50: ```tsx filename="app/products/[id]/page.tsx" switcher
51: import type { Metadata, ResolvingMetadata } from 'next'
52: 
53: type Props = {
54:   params: Promise<{ id: string }>
55:   searchParams: Promise<{ [key: string]: string | string[] | undefined }>
56: }
57: 
58: export async function generateMetadata(
59:   { params, searchParams }: Props,
60:   parent: ResolvingMetadata
61: ): Promise<Metadata> {
62:   // read route params
63:   const { id } = await params
64: 
65:   // fetch data
66:   const product = await fetch(`https://.../${id}`).then((res) => res.json())
67: 
68:   // optionally access and extend (rather than replace) parent metadata
69:   const previousImages = (await parent).openGraph?.images || []
70: 
71:   return {
72:     title: product.title,
73:     openGraph: {
74:       images: ['/some-specific-page-image.jpg', ...previousImages],
75:     },
76:   }
77: }
78: 
79: export default function Page({ params, searchParams }: Props) {}
80: ```
81: 
82: ```jsx filename="app/products/[id]/page.js" switcher
83: export async function generateMetadata({ params, searchParams }, parent) {
84:   // read route params
85:   const { id } = await params
86: 
87:   // fetch data
88:   const product = await fetch(`https://.../${id}`).then((res) => res.json())
89: 
90:   // optionally access and extend (rather than replace) parent metadata
91:   const previousImages = (await parent).openGraph?.images || []
92: 
93:   return {
94:     title: product.title,
95:     openGraph: {
96:       images: ['/some-specific-page-image.jpg', ...previousImages],
97:     },
98:   }
99: }
100: 
101: export default function Page({ params, searchParams }) {}
102: ```
103: 
104: For type completion of `params` and `searchParams`, you can type the first argument with [`PageProps<'/route'>`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#page-props-helper) or [`LayoutProps<'/route'>`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#layout-props-helper) for pages and layouts respectively.
105: 
106: > **Good to know**:
107: >
108: > - Metadata can be added to `layout.js` and `page.js` files.
109: > - Next.js will automatically resolve the metadata, and create the relevant `<head>` tags for the page.
110: > - The `metadata` object and `generateMetadata` function exports are **only supported in Server Components**.
111: > - You cannot export both the `metadata` object and `generateMetadata` function from the same route segment.
112: > - `fetch` requests inside `generateMetadata` are automatically [memoized](/docs/app/glossary#memoization) for the same data across `generateMetadata`, `generateStaticParams`, Layouts, Pages, and Server Components.
113: > - React [`cache` can be used](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) if `fetch` is unavailable.
114: > - [File-based metadata](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata) has the higher priority and will override the `metadata` object and `generateMetadata` function.
115: 
116: ## Why `generateMetadata` is Server Component only
117: 
118: `generateMetadata` and the `metadata` export are only supported in Server Components because metadata must be resolved on the server before the page component is rendered. This allows Next.js to include the metadata in the initial HTML response.
119: 
120: If you need to use Client Component features, keep your `page.tsx` as a Server Component and move the Client Component logic to a separate file:
121: 
122: ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
123: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
124: import { InteractiveComponent } from './interactive-component'
125: 
126: export const metadata: Metadata = {
127:   title: 'My Page',
128: }
129: 
130: export default function Page() {
131:   return <InteractiveComponent />
132: }
133: ```
134: 
135: ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
136: import { InteractiveComponent } from './interactive-component'
137: 
138: export const metadata = {
139:   title: 'My Page',
140: }
141: 
142: export default function Page() {
143:   return <InteractiveComponent />
144: }
145: ```
146: 
147: ```tsx filename="app/interactive-component.tsx" switcher
148: 'use client'
149: 
150: export function InteractiveComponent() {
151:   // Client-side interactivity (hooks, event handlers, etc.)
152: }
153: ```
154: 
155: ```jsx filename="app/interactive-component.js" switcher
156: 'use client'
157: 
158: export function InteractiveComponent() {
159:   // Client-side interactivity (hooks, event handlers, etc.)
160: }
161: ```
162: 
163: ## Reference
164: 
165: ### Parameters
166: 
167: `generateMetadata` function accepts the following parameters:
168: 
169: - `props` - An object containing the parameters of the current route:
170:   - `params` - An object containing the [dynamic route parameters](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes) object from the root segment down to the segment `generateMetadata` is called from. Examples:
171: 
172:     | Route                           | URL         | `params`                  |
173:     | ------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------- |
174:     | `app/shop/[slug]/page.js`       | `/shop/1`   | `{ slug: '1' }`           |
175:     | `app/shop/[tag]/[item]/page.js` | `/shop/1/2` | `{ tag: '1', item: '2' }` |
176:     | `app/shop/[...slug]/page.js`    | `/shop/1/2` | `{ slug: ['1', '2'] }`    |
177: 
178:   - `searchParams` - An object containing the current URL's [search params](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Learn/Common_questions/What_is_a_URL#parameters). Examples:
179: 
180:     | URL             | `searchParams`       |
181:     | --------------- | -------------------- |
182:     | `/shop?a=1`     | `{ a: '1' }`         |
183:     | `/shop?a=1&b=2` | `{ a: '1', b: '2' }` |
184:     | `/shop?a=1&a=2` | `{ a: ['1', '2'] }`  |
185: 
186: - `parent` - A promise of the resolved metadata from parent route segments.
187: 
188: ### Returns
189: 
190: `generateMetadata` should return a [`Metadata` object](#metadata-fields) containing one or more metadata fields.
191: 
192: > **Good to know**:
193: >
194: > - If metadata doesn't depend on request information, it should be defined using the static [`metadata` object](#the-metadata-object) rather than `generateMetadata`.
195: > - `fetch` requests are automatically memoized for the same data across `generateMetadata`, `generateStaticParams`, Layouts, Pages, and Server Components. React [`cache` can be used](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) if `fetch` is unavailable.
196: > - `searchParams` are only available in `page.js` segments.
197: > - The [`redirect()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/redirect) and [`notFound()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/not-found) Next.js methods can also be used inside `generateMetadata`.
198: 
199: ### Metadata Fields
200: 
201: The following fields are supported:
202: 
203: #### `title`
204: 
205: The `title` attribute is used to set the title of the document. It can be defined as a simple [string](#string) or an optional [template object](#template).
206: 
207: ##### String
208: 
209: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
210: export const metadata = {
211:   title: 'Next.js',
212: }
213: ```
214: 
215: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
216: <title>Next.js</title>
217: ```
218: 
219: ##### `default`
220: 
221: `title.default` can be used to provide a **fallback title** to child route segments that don't define a `title`.
222: 
223: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx"
224: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
225: 
226: export const metadata: Metadata = {
227:   title: {
228:     default: 'Acme',
229:   },
230: }
231: ```
232: 
233: ```tsx filename="app/about/page.tsx"
234: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
235: 
236: export const metadata: Metadata = {}
237: 
238: // Output: <title>Acme</title>
239: ```
240: 
241: ##### `template`
242: 
243: `title.template` can be used to add a prefix or a suffix to `titles` defined in **child** route segments.
244: 
245: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
246: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
247: 
248: export const metadata: Metadata = {
249:   title: {
250:     template: '%s | Acme',
251:     default: 'Acme', // a default is required when creating a template
252:   },
253: }
254: ```
255: 
256: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
257: export const metadata = {
258:   title: {
259:     template: '%s | Acme',
260:     default: 'Acme', // a default is required when creating a template
261:   },
262: }
263: ```
264: 
265: ```tsx filename="app/about/page.tsx" switcher
266: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
267: 
268: export const metadata: Metadata = {
269:   title: 'About',
270: }
271: 
272: // Output: <title>About | Acme</title>
273: ```
274: 
275: ```jsx filename="app/about/page.js" switcher
276: export const metadata = {
277:   title: 'About',
278: }
279: 
280: // Output: <title>About | Acme</title>
281: ```
282: 
283: > **Good to know**:
284: >
285: > - `title.template` applies to **child** route segments and **not** the segment it's defined in. This means:
286: >   - `title.default` is **required** when you add a `title.template`.
287: >   - `title.template` defined in `layout.js` will not apply to a `title` defined in a `page.js` of the same route segment.
288: >   - `title.template` defined in `page.js` has no effect because a page is always the terminating segment (it doesn't have any children route segments).
289: > - `title.template` has **no effect** if a route has not defined a `title` or `title.default`.
290: 
291: ##### `absolute`
292: 
293: `title.absolute` can be used to provide a title that **ignores** `title.template` set in parent segments.
294: 
295: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
296: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
297: 
298: export const metadata: Metadata = {
299:   title: {
300:     template: '%s | Acme',
301:   },
302: }
303: ```
304: 
305: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
306: export const metadata = {
307:   title: {
308:     template: '%s | Acme',
309:   },
310: }
311: ```
312: 
313: ```tsx filename="app/about/page.tsx" switcher
314: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
315: 
316: export const metadata: Metadata = {
317:   title: {
318:     absolute: 'About',
319:   },
320: }
321: 
322: // Output: <title>About</title>
323: ```
324: 
325: ```jsx filename="app/about/page.js" switcher
326: export const metadata = {
327:   title: {
328:     absolute: 'About',
329:   },
330: }
331: 
332: // Output: <title>About</title>
333: ```
334: 
335: > **Good to know**:
336: >
337: > - `layout.js`
338: >   - `title` (string) and `title.default` define the default title for child segments (that do not define their own `title`). It will augment `title.template` from the closest parent segment if it exists.
339: >   - `title.absolute` defines the default title for child segments. It ignores `title.template` from parent segments.
340: >   - `title.template` defines a new title template for child segments.
341: > - `page.js`
342: >   - If a page does not define its own title the closest parents resolved title will be used.
343: >   - `title` (string) defines the routes title. It will augment `title.template` from the closest parent segment if it exists.
344: >   - `title.absolute` defines the route title. It ignores `title.template` from parent segments.
345: >   - `title.template` has no effect in `page.js` because a page is always the terminating segment of a route.
346: 
347: ### `description`
348: 
349: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
350: export const metadata = {
351:   description: 'The React Framework for the Web',
352: }
353: ```
354: 
355: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
356: <meta name="description" content="The React Framework for the Web" />
357: ```
358: 
359: ### Other fields
360: 
361: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
362: export const metadata = {
363:   generator: 'Next.js',
364:   applicationName: 'Next.js',
365:   referrer: 'origin-when-cross-origin',
366:   keywords: ['Next.js', 'React', 'JavaScript'],
367:   authors: [{ name: 'Seb' }, { name: 'Josh', url: 'https://nextjs.org' }],
368:   creator: 'Jiachi Liu',
369:   publisher: 'Sebastian Markbåge',
370:   formatDetection: {
371:     email: false,
372:     address: false,
373:     telephone: false,
374:   },
375: }
376: ```
377: 
378: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
379: <meta name="application-name" content="Next.js" />
380: <meta name="author" content="Seb" />
381: <link rel="author" href="https://nextjs.org" />
382: <meta name="author" content="Josh" />

384: <meta name="keywords" content="Next.js,React,JavaScript" />
385: <meta name="referrer" content="origin-when-cross-origin" />
386: <meta name="color-scheme" content="dark" />
387: <meta name="creator" content="Jiachi Liu" />
388: <meta name="publisher" content="Sebastian Markbåge" />
389: <meta name="format-detection" content="telephone=no, address=no, email=no" />
390: ```
391: 
392: #### `metadataBase`
393: 
394: `metadataBase` is a convenience option to set a base URL prefix for `metadata` fields that require a fully qualified URL.
395: 
396: - `metadataBase` allows URL-based `metadata` fields defined in the **current route segment and below** to use a **relative path** instead of an otherwise required absolute URL.
397: - The field's relative path will be composed with `metadataBase` to form a fully qualified URL.
398: 
399: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
400: export const metadata = {
401:   metadataBase: new URL('https://acme.com'),
402:   alternates: {
403:     canonical: '/',
404:     languages: {
405:       'en-US': '/en-US',
406:       'de-DE': '/de-DE',
407:     },
408:   },
409:   openGraph: {
410:     images: '/og-image.png',
411:   },
412: }
413: ```
414: 
415: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
416: <link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.com" />
417: <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-US" href="https://acme.com/en-US" />
418: <link rel="alternate" hreflang="de-DE" href="https://acme.com/de-DE" />
419: <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.com/og-image.png" />
420: ```
421: 
422: > **Good to know**:
423: >
424: > - `metadataBase` is typically set in root `app/layout.js` to apply to URL-based `metadata` fields across all routes.
425: > - All URL-based `metadata` fields that require absolute URLs can be configured with a `metadataBase` option.
426: > - `metadataBase` can contain a subdomain e.g. `https://app.acme.com` or base path e.g. `https://acme.com/start/from/here`
427: > - If a `metadata` field provides an absolute URL, `metadataBase` will be ignored.
428: > - Using a relative path in a URL-based `metadata` field without configuring a `metadataBase` will cause a build error.
429: > - Next.js will normalize duplicate slashes between `metadataBase` (e.g. `https://acme.com/`) and a relative field (e.g. `/path`) to a single slash (e.g. `https://acme.com/path`)
430: 
431: #### URL Composition
432: 
433: URL composition favors developer intent over default directory traversal semantics.
434: 
435: - Trailing slashes between `metadataBase` and `metadata` fields are normalized.
436: - An "absolute" path in a `metadata` field (that typically would replace the whole URL path) is treated as a "relative" path (starting from the end of `metadataBase`).
437: 
438: For example, given the following `metadataBase`:
439: 
440: ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
441: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
442: 
443: export const metadata: Metadata = {
444:   metadataBase: new URL('https://acme.com'),
445: }
446: ```
447: 
448: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
449: export const metadata = {
450:   metadataBase: new URL('https://acme.com'),
451: }
452: ```
453: 
454: Any `metadata` fields that inherit the above `metadataBase` and set their own value will be resolved as follows:
455: 
456: | `metadata` field                 | Resolved URL                     |
457: | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
458: | `/`                              | `https://acme.com`               |
459: | `./`                             | `https://acme.com`               |
460: | `payments`                       | `https://acme.com/payments`      |
461: | `/payments`                      | `https://acme.com/payments`      |
462: | `./payments`                     | `https://acme.com/payments`      |
463: | `../payments`                    | `https://acme.com/payments`      |
464: | `https://beta.acme.com/payments` | `https://beta.acme.com/payments` |
465: 
466: ### `openGraph`
467: 
468: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
469: export const metadata = {
470:   openGraph: {
471:     title: 'Next.js',
472:     description: 'The React Framework for the Web',
473:     url: 'https://nextjs.org',
474:     siteName: 'Next.js',
475:     images: [
476:       {
477:         url: 'https://nextjs.org/og.png', // Must be an absolute URL
478:         width: 800,
479:         height: 600,
480:       },
481:       {
482:         url: 'https://nextjs.org/og-alt.png', // Must be an absolute URL
483:         width: 1800,
484:         height: 1600,
485:         alt: 'My custom alt',
486:       },
487:     ],
488:     videos: [
489:       {
490:         url: 'https://nextjs.org/video.mp4', // Must be an absolute URL
491:         width: 800,
492:         height: 600,
493:       },
494:     ],
495:     audio: [
496:       {
497:         url: 'https://nextjs.org/audio.mp3', // Must be an absolute URL
498:       },
499:     ],
500:     locale: 'en_US',
501:     type: 'website',
502:   },
503: }
504: ```
505: 
506: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
507: <meta property="og:title" content="Next.js" />
508: <meta property="og:description" content="The React Framework for the Web" />
509: <meta property="og:url" content="https://nextjs.org/" />
510: <meta property="og:site_name" content="Next.js" />
511: <meta property="og:locale" content="en_US" />
512: <meta property="og:image" content="https://nextjs.org/og.png" />
513: <meta property="og:image:width" content="800" />
514: <meta property="og:image:height" content="600" />
515: <meta property="og:image" content="https://nextjs.org/og-alt.png" />
516: <meta property="og:image:width" content="1800" />
517: <meta property="og:image:height" content="1600" />
518: <meta property="og:image:alt" content="My custom alt" />
519: <meta property="og:video" content="https://nextjs.org/video.mp4" />
520: <meta property="og:video:width" content="800" />
521: <meta property="og:video:height" content="600" />
522: <meta property="og:audio" content="https://nextjs.org/audio.mp3" />
523: <meta property="og:type" content="website" />
524: ```
525: 
526: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
527: export const metadata = {
528:   openGraph: {
529:     title: 'Next.js',
530:     description: 'The React Framework for the Web',
531:     type: 'article',
532:     publishedTime: '2023-01-01T00:00:00.000Z',
533:     authors: ['Seb', 'Josh'],
534:   },
535: }
536: ```
537: 
538: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
539: <meta property="og:title" content="Next.js" />
540: <meta property="og:description" content="The React Framework for the Web" />
541: <meta property="og:type" content="article" />
542: <meta property="article:published_time" content="2023-01-01T00:00:00.000Z" />
543: <meta property="article:author" content="Seb" />
544: <meta property="article:author" content="Josh" />
545: ```
546: 
547: > **Good to know**:
548: >
549: > - It may be more convenient to use the [file-based Metadata API](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image#image-files-jpg-png-gif) for Open Graph images. Rather than having to sync the config export with actual files, the file-based API will automatically generate the correct metadata for you.

567:       'max-snippet': -1,
568:     },
569:   },
570: }

581: ### `icons`
582: 
583: > **Good to know**: We recommend using the [file-based Metadata API](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons#image-files-ico-jpg-png) for icons where possible. Rather than having to sync the config export with actual files, the file-based API will automatically generate the correct metadata for you.
584: 
585: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
586: export const metadata = {
587:   icons: {
588:     icon: '/icon.png',
589:     shortcut: '/shortcut-icon.png',
590:     apple: '/apple-icon.png',
591:     other: {
592:       rel: 'apple-touch-icon-precomposed',
593:       url: '/apple-touch-icon-precomposed.png',
594:     },
595:   },
596: }
597: ```
598: 
599: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
600: <link rel="shortcut icon" href="/shortcut-icon.png" />
601: <link rel="icon" href="/icon.png" />
602: <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-icon.png" />
603: <link
604:   rel="apple-touch-icon-precomposed"
605:   href="/apple-touch-icon-precomposed.png"
606: />
607: ```
608: 
609: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
610: export const metadata = {
611:   icons: {
612:     icon: [
613:       { url: '/icon.png' },
614:       new URL('/icon.png', 'https://example.com'),
615:       { url: '/icon-dark.png', media: '(prefers-color-scheme: dark)' },
616:     ],
617:     shortcut: ['/shortcut-icon.png'],
618:     apple: [
619:       { url: '/apple-icon.png' },
620:       { url: '/apple-icon-x3.png', sizes: '180x180', type: 'image/png' },
621:     ],
622:     other: [
623:       {
624:         rel: 'apple-touch-icon-precomposed',
625:         url: '/apple-touch-icon-precomposed.png',
626:       },
627:     ],
628:   },
629: }
630: ```
631: 
632: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
633: <link rel="shortcut icon" href="/shortcut-icon.png" />
634: <link rel="icon" href="/icon.png" />
635: <link rel="icon" href="https://example.com/icon.png" />
636: <link rel="icon" href="/icon-dark.png" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" />
637: <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-icon.png" />
638: <link
639:   rel="apple-touch-icon-precomposed"
640:   href="/apple-touch-icon-precomposed.png"
641: />
642: <link
643:   rel="apple-touch-icon"
644:   href="/apple-icon-x3.png"
645:   sizes="180x180"
646:   type="image/png"
647: />
648: ```
649: 
650: > **Good to know**: The `msapplication-*` meta tags are no longer supported in Chromium builds of Microsoft Edge, and thus no longer needed.

674: ### `twitter`
675: 
676: The Twitter specification is (surprisingly) used for more than just X (formerly known as Twitter).
677: 
678: Learn more about the [Twitter Card markup reference](https://developer.x.com/en/docs/twitter-for-websites/cards/overview/markup).
679: 
680: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
681: export const metadata = {
682:   twitter: {
683:     card: 'summary_large_image',
684:     title: 'Next.js',
685:     description: 'The React Framework for the Web',
686:     siteId: '1467726470533754880',
687:     creator: '@nextjs',
688:     creatorId: '1467726470533754880',
689:     images: ['https://nextjs.org/og.png'], // Must be an absolute URL
690:   },
691: }
692: ```
693: 
694: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
695: <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image" />
696: <meta name="twitter:site:id" content="1467726470533754880" />
697: <meta name="twitter:creator" content="@nextjs" />
698: <meta name="twitter:creator:id" content="1467726470533754880" />
699: <meta name="twitter:title" content="Next.js" />
700: <meta name="twitter:description" content="The React Framework for the Web" />
701: <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://nextjs.org/og.png" />
702: ```
703: 
704: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
705: export const metadata = {
706:   twitter: {
707:     card: 'app',
708:     title: 'Next.js',
709:     description: 'The React Framework for the Web',
710:     siteId: '1467726470533754880',
711:     creator: '@nextjs',
712:     creatorId: '1467726470533754880',
713:     images: {
714:       url: 'https://nextjs.org/og.png',
715:       alt: 'Next.js Logo',
716:     },
717:     app: {
718:       name: 'twitter_app',
719:       id: {
720:         iphone: 'twitter_app://iphone',
721:         ipad: 'twitter_app://ipad',
722:         googleplay: 'twitter_app://googleplay',
723:       },
724:       url: {
725:         iphone: 'https://iphone_url',

727:       },
728:     },
729:   },
730: }
731: ```
732: 
733: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers

735: <meta name="twitter:creator" content="@nextjs" />
736: <meta name="twitter:creator:id" content="1467726470533754880" />
737: <meta name="twitter:title" content="Next.js" />
738: <meta name="twitter:description" content="The React Framework for the Web" />
739: <meta name="twitter:card" content="app" />
740: <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://nextjs.org/og.png" />

742: <meta name="twitter:app:name:iphone" content="twitter_app" />

745: <meta name="twitter:app:id:googleplay" content="twitter_app://googleplay" />
746: <meta name="twitter:app:url:iphone" content="https://iphone_url" />
747: <meta name="twitter:app:url:ipad" content="https://ipad_url" />

984: ### `pinterest`
985: 
986: You can enable or disable [Pinterest Rich Pins](https://developers.pinterest.com/docs/web-features/rich-pins-overview/) on your webpage.
987: 
988: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
989: export const metadata = {
990:   pinterest: {
991:     richPin: true,
992:   },
993: }
994: ```
995: 
996: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
997: <meta name="pinterest-rich-pin" content="true" />
998: ```
999: 
1000: ### `other`
1001: 
1002: All metadata options should be covered using the built-in support. However, there may be custom metadata tags specific to your site, or brand new metadata tags just released. You can use the `other` option to render any custom metadata tag.
1003: 
1004: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
1005: export const metadata = {
1006:   other: {
1007:     custom: 'meta',
1008:   },
1009: }
1010: ```
1011: 
1012: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
1013: <meta name="custom" content="meta" />
1014: ```
1015: 
1016: If you want to generate multiple same key meta tags you can use array value.
1017: 
1018: ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js"
1019: export const metadata = {
1020:   other: {
1021:     custom: ['meta1', 'meta2'],
1022:   },
1023: }
1024: ```
1025: 
1026: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
1027: <meta name="custom" content="meta1" /> <meta name="custom" content="meta2" />
1028: ```
1029: 
1030: ### Types
1031: 
1032: You can add type safety to your metadata by using the `Metadata` type. If you are using the [built-in TypeScript plugin](/docs/app/api-reference/config/typescript) in your IDE, you do not need to manually add the type, but you can still explicitly add it if you want.
1033: 
1034: #### `metadata` object
1035: 
1036: ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx"
1037: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
1038: 
1039: export const metadata: Metadata = {
1040:   title: 'Next.js',
1041: }
1042: ```
1043: 
1044: #### `generateMetadata` function
1045: 
1046: ##### Regular function
1047: 
1048: ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx"
1049: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
1050: 
1051: export function generateMetadata(): Metadata {
1052:   return {
1053:     title: 'Next.js',
1054:   }
1055: }
1056: ```
1057: 
1058: ##### Async function
1059: 
1060: ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx"
1061: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
1062: 
1063: export async function generateMetadata(): Promise<Metadata> {
1064:   return {
1065:     title: 'Next.js',
1066:   }
1067: }
1068: ```
1069: 
1070: ##### With segment props
1071: 
1072: ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx"
1073: import type { Metadata } from 'next'
1074: 
1075: type Props = {
1076:   params: Promise<{ id: string }>
1077:   searchParams: Promise<{ [key: string]: string | string[] | undefined }>
1078: }
1079: 
1080: export function generateMetadata({ params, searchParams }: Props): Metadata {
1081:   return {
1082:     title: 'Next.js',
1083:   }
1084: }
1085: 
1086: export default function Page({ params, searchParams }: Props) {}
1087: ```
1088: 
1089: ##### With parent metadata
1090: 
1091: ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx"
1092: import type { Metadata, ResolvingMetadata } from 'next'
1093: 
1094: export async function generateMetadata(
1095:   { params, searchParams }: Props,
1096:   parent: ResolvingMetadata
1097: ): Promise<Metadata> {
1098:   return {
1099:     title: 'Next.js',
1100:   }
1101: }
1102: ```
1103: 
1104: ##### JavaScript Projects
1105: 
1106: For JavaScript projects, you can use JSDoc to add type safety.
1107: 
1108: ```js filename="layout.js | page.js"
1109: /** @type {import("next").Metadata} */
1110: export const metadata = {
1111:   title: 'Next.js',
1112: }
1113: ```
1114: 
1115: ### Unsupported Metadata
1116: 
1117: The following metadata types do not currently have built-in support. However, they can still be rendered in the layout or page itself.
1118: 
1119: | Metadata                      | Recommendation                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
1120: | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
1121: | `<meta http-equiv="...">`     | Use appropriate HTTP Headers via [`redirect()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/redirect), [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#nextresponse), [Security Headers](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/headers) |
1122: | `<base>`                      | Render the tag in the layout or page itself.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
1123: | `<noscript>`                  | Render the tag in the layout or page itself.                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
1124: | `<style>`                     | Learn more about [styling in Next.js](/docs/app/getting-started/css).                                                                                                                                                                        |
1125: | `<script>`                    | Learn more about [using scripts](/docs/app/guides/scripts).                                                                                                                                                                                  |
1126: | `<link rel="stylesheet" />`   | `import` stylesheets directly in the layout or page itself.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
1127: | `<link rel="preload />`       | Use [ReactDOM preload method](#link-relpreload)                                                                                                                                                                                              |
1128: | `<link rel="preconnect" />`   | Use [ReactDOM preconnect method](#link-relpreconnect)                                                                                                                                                                                        |
1129: | `<link rel="dns-prefetch" />` | Use [ReactDOM prefetchDNS method](#link-reldns-prefetch)                                                                                                                                                                                     |
1130: 
1131: ### Resource hints
1132: 
1133: The `<link>` element has a number of `rel` keywords that can be used to hint to the browser that an external resource is likely to be needed. The browser uses this information to apply preloading optimizations depending on the keyword.
1134: 
1135: While the Metadata API doesn't directly support these hints, you can use new [`ReactDOM` methods](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/26237) to safely insert them into the `<head>` of the document.
1136: 
1137: ```tsx filename="app/preload-resources.tsx" switcher
1138: 'use client'
1139: 
1140: import ReactDOM from 'react-dom'
1141: 
1142: export function PreloadResources() {
1143:   ReactDOM.preload('...', { as: '...' })
1144:   ReactDOM.preconnect('...', { crossOrigin: '...' })
1145:   ReactDOM.prefetchDNS('...')
1146: 
1147:   return '...'
1148: }
1149: ```
1150: 
1151: ```jsx filename="app/preload-resources.js" switcher
1152: 'use client'
1153: 
1154: import ReactDOM from 'react-dom'
1155: 
1156: export function PreloadResources() {
1157:   ReactDOM.preload('...', { as: '...' })
1158:   ReactDOM.preconnect('...', { crossOrigin: '...' })
1159:   ReactDOM.prefetchDNS('...')
1160: 
1161:   return '...'
1162: }
1163: ```
1164: 
1165: #### `<link rel="preload">`
1166: 
1167: Start loading a resource early in the page rendering (browser) lifecycle. [MDN Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel/preload).
1168: 
1169: ```tsx
1170: ReactDOM.preload(href: string, options: { as: string })
1171: ```
1172: 
1173: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
1174: <link rel="preload" href="..." as="..." />
1175: ```
1176: 
1177: ##### `<link rel="preconnect">`
1178: 
1179: Preemptively initiate a connection to an origin. [MDN Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel/preconnect).
1180: 
1181: ```tsx
1182: ReactDOM.preconnect(href: string, options?: { crossOrigin?: string })
1183: ```
1184: 
1185: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
1186: <link rel="preconnect" href="..." crossorigin />
1187: ```
1188: 
1189: #### `<link rel="dns-prefetch">`
1190: 
1191: Attempt to resolve a domain name before resources get requested. [MDN Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel/dns-prefetch).
1192: 
1193: ```tsx
1194: ReactDOM.prefetchDNS(href: string)
1195: ```
1196: 
1197: ```html filename="<head> output" hideLineNumbers
1198: <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="..." />
1199: ```
1200: 
1201: > **Good to know**:
1202: >
1203: > - These methods are currently only supported in Client Components, which are still Server Side Rendered on initial page load.
1204: > - Next.js in-built features such as `next/font`, `next/image` and `next/script` automatically handle relevant resource hints.
1205: 
1206: ## Behavior
1207: 
1208: ### Default Fields
1209: 
1210: There are two default `meta` tags that are always added even if a route doesn't define metadata:
1211: 
1212: - The [meta charset tag](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Element/meta#attr-charset) sets the character encoding for the website.
1213: - The [meta viewport tag](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Viewport_meta_tag) sets the viewport width and scale for the website to adjust for different devices.
1214: 
1215: ```html
1216: <meta charset="utf-8" />
1217: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
1218: ```
1219: 
1220: > **Good to know**: You can overwrite the default [`viewport`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#viewport) meta tag.
1221: 
1222: ### Streaming metadata
1223: 
1224: Streaming metadata allows Next.js to render and send the initial UI to the browser, without waiting for `generateMetadata` to complete.
1225: 
1226: When `generateMetadata` resolves, the resulting metadata tags are appended to the `<body>` tag. We have verified that metadata is interpreted correctly by bots that execute JavaScript and inspect the full DOM (e.g. `Googlebot`).
1227: 
1228: For **HTML-limited bots** that can’t execute JavaScript (e.g. `facebookexternalhit`), metadata continues to block page rendering. The resulting metadata will be available in the `<head>` tag.
1229: 
1230: Next.js automatically detects **HTML-limited bots** by looking at the User Agent header. You can use the [`htmlLimitedBots`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/htmlLimitedBots) option in your Next.js config file to override the default [User Agent list](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/utils/html-bots.ts).
1231: 
1232: To fully disable streaming metadata:
1233: 
1234: ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher
1235: import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
1236: 
1237: const config: NextConfig = {
1238:   htmlLimitedBots: /.*/,
1239: }
1240: 
1241: export default config
1242: ```
1243: 
1244: ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher
1245: module.exports = {
1246:   htmlLimitedBots: /.*/,
1247: }
1248: ```
1249: 
1250: Streaming metadata improves perceived performance by reducing [TTFB](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Glossary/Time_to_first_byte) and can help lowering [LCP](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Glossary/Largest_contentful_paint) time.
1251: 
1252: Overriding `htmlLimitedBots` could lead to longer response times. Streaming metadata is an advanced feature, and the default should be sufficient for most cases.
1253: 
1254: ### With Cache Components
1255: 
1256: When [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) is enabled, `generateMetadata` follows the same rules as other components. If metadata accesses runtime data (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `params`, `searchParams`) or performs uncached data fetching, it defers to request time.
1257: 
1258: How Next.js handles this depends on the rest of your page:
1259: 
1260: - **If other parts also defer to request time**: Prerendering generates a static shell, and metadata streams in with other deferred content.
1261: - **If the page or layout is otherwise fully prerenderable**: Next.js requires an explicit choice: cache the data if possible, or signal that deferred rendering is intentional.
1262: 
1263: Streaming metadata at runtime while the rest of the page is fully prerenderable is not common. To ensure this behavior is intentional, an error is raised indicating which page or layout needs to be handled.
1264: 
1265: To resolve this, you have two options. If metadata depends on external data but not runtime data, use `use cache`:
1266: 
1267: ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={2}
1268: export async function generateMetadata() {
1269:   'use cache'
1270:   const { title, description } = await db.query('site-metadata')
1271:   return { title, description }
1272: }
1273: ```
1274: 
1275: If metadata genuinely requires runtime data, add a dynamic marker component to your page:
1276: 
1277: ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={11-14,19,31}
1278: import { Suspense } from 'react'
1279: import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
1280: import { connection } from 'next/server'
1281: 
1282: export async function generateMetadata() {
1283:   const token = (await cookies()).get('token')?.value
1284:   // ... use token to fetch personalized metadata
1285:   return { title: 'Personalized Title' }
1286: }
1287: 
1288: const Connection = async () => {
1289:   await connection()
1290:   return null
1291: }
1292: 
1293: async function DynamicMarker() {
1294:   return (
1295:     <Suspense>
1296:       <Connection />
1297:     </Suspense>
1298:   )
1299: }
1300: 
1301: export default function Page() {
1302:   // DO NOT place await connection() here
1303:   // doing so prevents the article tag content from
1304:   // being included in the static shell
1305:   return (
1306:     <>
1307:       <article>Static content</article>
1308:       <DynamicMarker />
1309:     </>
1310:   )
1311: }
1312: ```
1313: 
1314: The `DynamicMarker` component renders nothing but tells Next.js the page has intentional dynamic content. By wrapping it in Suspense, the static content still prerenders normally.
1315: 
1316: See [Next.js encountered runtime data in `generateMetadata()`](/docs/messages/blocking-prerender-metadata-runtime) and [Next.js encountered uncached data in `generateMetadata()`](/docs/messages/blocking-prerender-metadata-dynamic) for full fix options and trade-offs.
1317: 
1318: ### Ordering
1319: 
1320: Metadata is evaluated in order, starting from the root segment down to the segment closest to the final `page.js` segment. For example:
1321: 
1322: 1. `app/layout.tsx` (Root Layout)
1323: 2. `app/blog/layout.tsx` (Nested Blog Layout)
1324: 3. `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` (Blog Page)
1325: 
1326: ### Merging
1327: 
1328: Following the [evaluation order](#ordering), Metadata objects exported from multiple segments in the same route are **shallowly** merged together to form the final metadata output of a route. Duplicate keys are **replaced** based on their ordering.
1329: 
1330: This means metadata with nested fields such as [`openGraph`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#opengraph) and [`robots`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#robots) that are defined in an earlier segment are **overwritten** by the last segment to define them.
1331: 
1332: #### Overwriting fields
1333: 
1334: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js"
1335: export const metadata = {
1336:   title: 'Acme',
1337:   openGraph: {
1338:     title: 'Acme',
1339:     description: 'Acme is a...',
1340:   },
1341: }
1342: ```
1343: 
1344: ```jsx filename="app/blog/page.js"
1345: export const metadata = {
1346:   title: 'Blog',
1347:   openGraph: {
1348:     title: 'Blog',
1349:   },
1350: }
1351: 
1352: // Output:
1353: // <title>Blog</title>
1354: // <meta property="og:title" content="Blog" />
1355: ```
1356: 
1357: In the example above:
1358: 
1359: - `title` from `app/layout.js` is **replaced** by `title` in `app/blog/page.js`.
1360: - All `openGraph` fields from `app/layout.js` are **replaced** in `app/blog/page.js` because `app/blog/page.js` sets `openGraph` metadata. Note the absence of `openGraph.description`.
1361: 
1362: If you'd like to share some nested fields between segments while overwriting others, you can pull them out into a separate variable:
1363: 
1364: ```jsx filename="app/shared-metadata.js"
1365: export const openGraphImage = { images: ['http://...'] }
1366: ```
1367: 
1368: ```jsx filename="app/page.js"
1369: import { openGraphImage } from './shared-metadata'
1370: 
1371: export const metadata = {
1372:   openGraph: {
1373:     ...openGraphImage,
1374:     title: 'Home',
1375:   },
1376: }
1377: ```
1378: 
1379: ```jsx filename="app/about/page.js"
1380: import { openGraphImage } from '../shared-metadata'
1381: 
1382: export const metadata = {
1383:   openGraph: {
1384:     ...openGraphImage,
1385:     title: 'About',
1386:   },
1387: }
1388: ```
1389: 
1390: In the example above, the OG image is shared between `app/layout.js` and `app/about/page.js` while the titles are different.
1391: 
1392: #### Inheriting fields
1393: 
1394: ```jsx filename="app/layout.js"
1395: export const metadata = {
1396:   title: 'Acme',
1397:   openGraph: {
1398:     title: 'Acme',
1399:     description: 'Acme is a...',
1400:   },
1401: }
1402: ```
1403: 
1404: ```jsx filename="app/about/page.js"
1405: export const metadata = {
1406:   title: 'About',
1407: }
1408: 
1409: // Output:
1410: // <title>About</title>
1411: // <meta property="og:title" content="Acme" />
1412: // <meta property="og:description" content="Acme is a..." />
1413: ```
1414: 
1415: **Notes**
1416: 
1417: - `title` from `app/layout.js` is **replaced** by `title` in `app/about/page.js`.
1418: - All `openGraph` fields from `app/layout.js` are **inherited** in `app/about/page.js` because `app/about/page.js` doesn't set `openGraph` metadata.
1419: 
1420: ## Version History
1421: 
1422: | Version   | Changes                                                                                                                                                 |
1423: | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
1424: | `v15.2.0` | Introduced streaming support to `generateMetadata`.                                                                                                     |
1425: | `v13.2.0` | `viewport`, `themeColor`, and `colorScheme` deprecated in favor of the [`viewport` configuration](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-viewport). |
1426: | `v13.2.0` | `metadata` and `generateMetadata` introduced.                                                                                                           |

# Skill: tdd

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams — where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled** — mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological** — the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth — a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing** — writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead — one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

# Skill: code-review

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards** — does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec** — does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / PRD / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point — a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc. If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here — not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.) — fetch via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A PRD/spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below — a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation — and, like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name** — a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code** — the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy** — a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps** — the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession** — a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches** — the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery** — one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change** — one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality** — abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains** — long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man** — a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest** — a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

Send a single message with two `Agent` tool calls. Use the `general-purpose` subagent for both.

**Standards sub-agent prompt** — include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full — the sub-agent has no other access to it.
- The brief: "Report — per file/hunk where relevant — (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls — documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** — include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings — the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes — that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

+export function findMaterialSourceConflicts(label: ProductLabel): string[] {
+  const routes = label.metadata.regulatory
+    .filter((field) => field.name === "route")
+    .flatMap((field) => field.values.map(String));
+  const dosageText = [
+    ...usefulFragments(label.dosageAndAdministration),
+    ...usefulFragments(label.dosageAndAdministrationTable),
+  ]
+    .join(" ")
+    .toLowerCase();
+
+  if (!dosageText) {
+    return [];
+  }
+
+  const hasSolidDoseInstructions = /\b(?:tablet|tablets|caplet|caplets|pill|pills)\b/.test(
+    dosageText,
+  );
+  const hasTopicalInstructions =
+    /\b(?:apply|cream|ointment|skin|topical)\b/.test(dosageText);
+
+  return routes.flatMap((route) => {
+    const normalizedRoute = route.toLowerCase();
+    const conflicts =
+      (normalizedRoute.includes("topical") && hasSolidDoseInstructions) ||
+      (normalizedRoute.includes("oral") && hasTopicalInstructions) ||
+      (/(intravenous|intramuscular|subcutaneous)/.test(normalizedRoute) &&
+        hasSolidDoseInstructions);
+
+    return conflicts
+      ? [
+          `Source conflict: route metadata lists ${sentenceCase(route)}, while dosage text mentions ${hasSolidDoseInstructions ? "tablet or caplet instructions" : "topical application instructions"}. The directory displays both source values and does not correct or clinically validate them.`,
+        ]
+      : [];
+  });
+}

+    .toLowerCase()

+}

+export function findMaterialSourceConflicts(label: ProductLabel): string[] {
+  const routes = label.metadata.regulatory
+    .filter((field) => field.name === "route")
+    .flatMap((field) => field.values.map(String));
+  const dosageText = [
+    ...usefulFragments(label.dosageAndAdministration),
+    ...usefulFragments(label.dosageAndAdministrationTable),
+  ]
+    .join(" ")
+    .toLowerCase();
+
+  if (!dosageText) {
+    return [];
+  }
+
+  const hasSolidDoseInstructions = containsUnnegatedPhrase(
+    dosageText,
+    /\b(?:tablet|tablets|caplet|caplets|pill|pills)\b/g,
+  );
+  const hasOralInstructions = containsUnnegatedPhrase(
+    dosageText,
+    /\b(?:by mouth|orally|swallow)\b/g,
+  );
+  const hasTopicalInstructions = containsUnnegatedPhrase(
+    dosageText,
+    /\b(?:apply|cream|ointment|skin|topical)\b/g,
+  );
+
+  return routes.flatMap((route) => {
+    const normalizedRoute = route.toLowerCase();
+    const topicalRoute = /\b(?:topical|dermal|cutaneous)\b/.test(
+      normalizedRoute,
+    );
+    const oralRoute = /\b(?:oral|buccal|sublingual)\b/.test(normalizedRoute);
+    const nonOralRoute = /\b(?:intravenous|intramuscular|subcutaneous|ophthalmic|otic|nasal|inhalation)\b/.test(
+      normalizedRoute,
+    );
+    const conflicts =
+      (topicalRoute && (hasSolidDoseInstructions || hasOralInstructions)) ||
+      (oralRoute && hasTopicalInstructions) ||
+      (nonOralRoute && (hasSolidDoseInstructions || hasOralInstructions));
+    const dosageDescription = hasSolidDoseInstructions
+      ? "solid oral dosage instructions"
+      : hasOralInstructions
+        ? "oral dosage instructions"
+        : "topical application instructions";
+
+    return conflicts
+      ? [
+          `Source conflict: route metadata lists ${sentenceCase(route)}, while dosage text mentions ${dosageDescription}. The directory displays both source values and does not correct or clinically validate them.`,
+        ]
+      : [];
+  });
+}
+
+function containsUnnegatedPhrase(value: string, pattern: RegExp): boolean {
+  for (const match of value.matchAll(pattern)) {
+    const matchIndex = match.index ?? 0;
+    const precedingText = value.slice(Math.max(0, matchIndex - 24), matchIndex);
+
+    if (!/\b(?:do not|don't|not)\b[\w\s]{0,18}$/.test(precedingText)) {
+      return true;
+    }
+  }
+
+  return false;
+}
+
 export function deriveDosageTable(
   fragment: string,
 ): DerivedTableView | undefined {
@@ -406,6 +474,12 @@ function decodeEntities(value: string): string {
   );
 }
 
+function sentenceCase(value: string): string {
+  return value
+    .toLowerCase()
+    .replace(/\b\w/g, (character) => character.toUpperCase());
+}

 function isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> {

## User

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

I want to redesign the visual style of this app - not the content or domain 
logic, just the look and feel. Right now it uses a serif, editorial style. 
I want it to look like a trusted Indian medical/health platform, in the 
style of Apollo Pharmacy - clean, clinical, trustworthy, mobile-first.

Before making changes, read CONTEXT.md and docs/adr/ to remind yourself of 
the domain decisions already made (set_id identity, safety field 
independence, US-vs-India disclaimer, route/form badges, etc.) - none of 
that logic should change, only how it's presented.

Color palette to use:
- Primary (deep teal): #1B4B43 - for header, nav, primary buttons, "Open 
  Product" links, active states
- Accent (warm coral/orange): #E8622C - for badges (route/form), highlights, 
  non-safety icons
- Safety/danger (distinct from accent): #B23A2E - specifically for the 
  Safety Fields warning icon and any safety-related emphasis, so it stays 
  visually distinct from the general accent color
- Background: #FFFFFF / #FAFAF9 (off-white)
- Card surfaces: white with a hairline border in #E5E5E0
- Text primary: #1A1A1A
- Text secondary: #6B6B68

Specific direction:
1. Switch to a clean sans-serif typeface throughout instead of the current 
   serif headings.
2. Apply the color palette above consistently - primary teal for structural/
   navigation elements and buttons, coral accent for badges and highlights, 
   the separate danger red only for safety warnings.
3. Give the search bar a "health app" feel - rounded input, a search icon 
   inside the field, teal-bordered focus state.
4. On the product page, keep the existing content hierarchy (badges, 
   collapsible sections, safety fields, disclaimers) but restyle cards to 
   look more like a clinical record - consistent card elevation, icons per 
   section (pill icon for ingredients, shield/alert icon in the danger red 
   for safety, info icon for regulatory metadata), tighter and more 
   scannable spacing.
5. Keep all existing collapsible behavior, badges, and disclaimers exactly 
   as they function now - this is a visual/styling pass only.

This is presentation-only - don't touch data fetching, types, tests, or any 
domain logic. Only page.tsx files, component styling, and globals.css/theme 
tokens should change. Confirm which files you touched when done.
